The film opens at the close of the Antarctic summer, when every penguin of breeding age leaves the ocean and walks inland, single file, to an ancestral breeding ground on solid, year-round ice. By the end of winter that site lies more than 100 kilometres from open water. After courtship, each female lays a single egg and passes it to her mate's feet with as little exposure to the cold as possible, then sets off back to the sea to feed, having lost a third of her body weight. The males, who by then have gone two months without food, huddle together through the polar winter to incubate the eggs in temperatures nearing −62 °C, drinking only fallen snow.

When the chicks hatch, the fathers can offer only a small meal secreted from a throat sac, and they must abandon their young if the mothers fail to return. The returning females recognise their families by their calls and take over feeding, while the starving males make the long trek to the ocean. Storms kill some chicks, a grieving mother tries to steal another's young, and predators such as leopard seals and giant petrels take their toll on adults and chicks alike. As spring advances and the ice melts, the trips grow shorter, until the parents finally leave the chicks to fend for themselves.

Scorsese filmed two benefit shows on 29 October and 1 November 2006, both added to the tour specifically for the shoot, although all the concert footage in the final cut comes from the second night. The concert is preceded by a brief, partly staged prologue showing the preparations showing the director and his crew getting ready for the shoot, and the music is intercut with archival news clips and old interviews with Jagger, Keith Richards, Charlie Watts and Ronnie Wood that trace the band's long career and its reputation for excess and endurance. Guest performers join the band on stage, including Jack White, the blues guitarist Buddy Guy and Christina Aguilera, while backing musicians such as Blondie Chaplin and Tim Ries also appear. The audience included Bill and Hillary Clinton, and the concerts raised money for the Clinton Foundation. The set list differed from the usual tour shows, and Jagger joked that this might be the only Scorsese film without "Gimme Shelter". Before the first show, Atlantic Records co-founder Ahmet Ertegun fell backstage and later died from his injuries, and the film is dedicated to him.

The story is set in Treasure Town, a sprawling, ageing city of alleys and rooftops that is changing fast under pressure from the yakuza and outside speculators. Two orphaned boys, the hardened, violent Black and the dreamy, childlike White, live there as street kids who treat the town as their own territory and defend it against all comers, while dreaming of a house by the sea. Their world is upended when a ruthless outsider known as the Snake arrives with plans to tear down the old neighbourhood and replace it with a vast amusement park, backed by three uncanny, seemingly unstoppable assassins. Under this pressure the brothers are separated: White is taken into the care of two police detectives, while Black, cut off from the one person who anchors him, sinks deeper into violence and confronts a darker side of himself embodied by a figure called the Minotaur. In the end it is the bond between the brothers that pulls him back.

The Japanese voice cast is led by Kazunari Ninomiya as Black and Yū Aoi as White, with Yūsuke Iseya as the yakuza Kimura, Kankurō Kudō and Min Tanaka, who voices the old gangster known as the Rat, and Masahiro Motoki as the Snake. The score is by the British electronic duo Plaid, with a closing song by Asian Kung-Fu Generation.

The documentary traces the history of The Matrix from its development and pre-production through filming and post-production to its release. It explains how some of the film's most complicated scenes were achieved, including its groundbreaking visual effects, and covers set construction and stunt work. Among the anecdotes it offers are that Reeves had to undergo neck surgery while making the film and that the Wachowskis had their star read philosophy before shooting. The program also offered audiences an early look at the two sequels then in production, The Matrix Reloaded and The Matrix Revolutions, both released in 2003. Alongside the main documentary, the disc included featurettes on the sequels, the comic books inspired by the film, the official website and the fan community, on the building of particular sets and sequences, on the special effects, and Yuen Woo-ping's test footage for the kung fu scenes. An Easter egg in the language menu, reached by highlighting a telephone booth, gave access to a jukebox of 41 techno tracks used in the documentary.

Initially issued as a stand-alone title, the documentary was later included in a two-disc collector's edition of The Matrix and became part of The Ultimate Matrix Collection box set. Reviewers were generally appreciative. The DVD Journal welcomed Warner's decision to release the supplements separately, so that owners of the popular original disc, criticized for its weak extras, did not have to replace it. It judged the documentary better than standard electronic press kits and pleasantly light on film clips, though not as engaging as the best behind-the-scenes accounts such as Hearts of Darkness, and noted the absence of some cast members, including Joe Pantoliano. Other reviewers found it thorough, though some considered it largely promotional.

Some time after the defeat of the Chitauri, Captain America continues to fly missions for S.H.I.E.L.D. but is haunted by memories of Kleiser, the shape-shifting alien commander he fought in the Second World War, and takes increasingly reckless risks. In the isolated African kingdom of Wakanda, Kleiser resurfaces and the Chitauri attack, killing the king, T'Chaka. The invaders are after vibranium, a metal found only in Wakanda that they use to build their ships and weapons. Prince T'Challa assumes his father's mantle as the Black Panther and, defying his nation's sacred tradition of isolation from outsiders, seeks out Captain America for help.

Nick Fury reassembles the team, though Thor is initially unavailable and Bruce Banner remains under guard. A misunderstanding with Wakandan soldiers leaves the Wasp injured and Captain America's shield stolen, but the heroes, now joined by Thor, unite with the Black Panther against the Chitauri. From his confinement, Banner works out that gamma radiation weakens vibranium and sends Betty Ross to Wakanda with a gamma-ray projector. The weapon cripples the invaders, and Iron Man and Giant-Man destroy the power core of the Chitauri mothership, though Giant-Man is fatally wounded. After the Black Panther thanks his allies, the team returns home to learn that Banner has transformed into the Hulk and escaped.

The voice cast includes Justin Gross as Captain America, Marc Worden as Iron Man, Olivia d'Abo as Black Widow, Michael Massee as Bruce Banner with Fred Tatasciore as the Hulk, David Boat as Thor, Andre Ware as Nick Fury and Jeffrey D. Sams as the Black Panther, alongside Grey DeLisle and Nolan North. The film was later broadcast on Cartoon Network's Toonami block and received a mixed critical response.

Stephen Strange is a gifted but arrogant neurosurgeon who takes only prestigious cases. Driving home one night, he glimpses Baron Mordo and other warriors slaying a monster in the street, but dismisses it as stress. His former lover, Dr. Gina Atwater, asks for his help with a ward of children trapped in comas and plagued by nightmares; when one child touches him, he sees a skull wreathed in flames and walks away. On the drive home, ghostly visions cause him to crash, and his hands are crushed. Strange spends everything he has on failed treatments, and when he tries to end his life, he is stopped by the mysterious Wong, who tells him that healing may await in Tibet.

At a hidden Himalayan monastery, Strange trains under the Ancient One, whose acolytes battle a growing wave of mystical creatures. He confronts his guilt over the death of his sister April, who died while he operated on her brain tumor, and the Ancient One names him the true heir to the title of Sorcerer Supreme, enraging the ambitious Mordo. Strange learns that the demon Dormammu, long imprisoned in another dimension, is using the dreaming children to break into Earth. While Strange wakes the children, Mordo betrays the order and pledges himself to Dormammu, and the Ancient One dies after an attack. Wong gives Strange the Eye of Agamotto, and Strange defeats Mordo, but Dormammu devours the traitor and emerges. Strange then absorbs the demon's pure magic until it fades away. As the new Sorcerer Supreme, he reassures Gina in a dream and bids farewell at his sister's grave.

The film aired on Cartoon Network in 2008. Reviews were mixed: IGN praised its action and emotional resonance, while DVD Talk criticized its changes to the character and Johnson's voice work. It earned an Annie Award nomination.

The Canadian agency Department H sends Wolverine to track down the Hulk, a creature blamed for destroying the town of Elkford in British Columbia. Surveying the ruins, Wolverine picks up a strange chemical scent and the smell of gunpowder before heading into the wilderness after his quarry. The two collide in a savage, prolonged brawl that ends only when both are knocked out by tranquiliser darts. They wake as prisoners of Weapon X, the secret programme that once bonded adamantium to Wolverine's skeleton and conditioned him as a living weapon, scenes revealed in flashbacks to his escape years earlier. Its leader, a scientist known as the Professor, explains that his own soldiers, not the Hulk, wrecked Elkford while hunting the creature, and that he intends to erase Bruce Banner's mind and reprogram the Hulk as the most powerful weapon on Earth.

Wolverine breaks free, frees Banner and fights his way through his former teammates of Team X: Sabretooth, Lady Deathstrike, Omega Red and the wisecracking mercenary Deadpool. When the drugged Banner cannot transform on his own, Wolverine provokes the change by force, and the unleashed Hulk smashes the assassins and the facility, which collapses in an explosion. Emerging from the flames, Hulk and Wolverine square off to resume their fight, and a scene after the credits shows a battered Deadpool surviving the wreckage.

The voice cast includes Steve Blum as Wolverine, Fred Tatasciore as the Hulk, Bryce Johnson as Banner, Nolan North as Deadpool, Tom Kane as the Professor, Mark Acheson, Janyse Jaud and Colin Murdock. First screened at San Diego Comic-Con in 2008, the film was praised for its intense action, unusually bloody violence for a Marvel cartoon and Deadpool's scene-stealing humour, though some reviewers found the Weapon X backstory a distraction from the title bout.

In a dream, the ghost of François's grandmother warns him not to let his curiosity take control of him, while two black-clad fallen angels hover over him as he sleeps, conspiring to set events in motion. François plans a film about the moment when women transgress sexual taboos. Without a producer or casting director, he holds auditions himself, and after many candidates refuse, two young actresses show promise. In a restaurant he guides Charlotte through an improvisation in which she pleasures herself among the diners, joined by Julie, as the waitress Stéphanie looks on; the trio continues the experiment in a hotel. The next day Stéphanie comes to his office and asks to take part. François insists he is only gathering material for his script and remains a detached observer, but the encounters become increasingly intense. Charlotte grows obsessive, wrecking her apartment and calling him at all hours, and his wife warns him about her ego, while the women's rivalries and obsessions, apparently steered by the spirits, turn against him with tragic consequences.

Twenty years after the death of Arthur and the fall of Camelot, the castle is ruled by the sorcerer Arkadian, who draws his power from the Book of Beasts, a magical tome that unleashes monstrous creatures. Avlynn sets out with the last of the knights, among them Sir Galahad, his son Lysanor and Tristan, to find Merlin, Arthur's old counsellor, now living as a recluse in an enchanted forest and known as the wild man of the woods. Merlin at first refuses to help, but eventually joins the quest to retake Camelot, which also requires Avlynn to find Excalibur. Arkadian is revealed to be Mordred, Arthur's son by Morgan le Fay and thus Avlynn's half-brother.

Along the way Merlin is struck down, and the company carries him to a legendary healing well, only to find it dry. Galahad urges them to leave him behind, but Avlynn refuses and draws water from the well with her own blood, reviving the wizard, who then dispatches a pack of Medusa-like creatures sent by Arkadian. At the Lake of Destiny Avlynn recovers her father's sword, before the group is captured by giant birds under the sorcerer's control. Arkadian tries to seduce Avlynn by taking on the appearance of Lysanor, with whom she is in love. In the final battle Merlin strips Arkadian of his magic and binds his spirit within Camelot, while Avlynn uses Excalibur to pin the Book of Beasts to a rock, saving Merlin from being consumed by it.

While the Straw Hat Pirates relax on a beach, their ship, the Going Merry, is stolen before their eyes along with their belongings, forcing them to sail in a swan boat and wear rented wedding outfits. They meet the self-proclaimed Thief Brothers, Borodo and his younger companion Akisu, who suggest that the culprits are the Trump Pirates, a gang led by five siblings themed after playing cards. During the search, Nami is kidnapped to become the bride of their captain, Bear King, and the crew follows her captors to their base, Clockwork Island, a mechanical isle that Bear King seized years earlier, forcing its inhabitants to build weapons for him. One by one, Sanji, Usopp and Zoro are captured or defeated.

Borodo eventually confesses that he stole the Merry and handed it to the pirates to push Luffy into fighting them; his true aim is to free the islanders and return Akisu, who was set adrift as a baby, to his parents. Encouraged by Usopp, Akisu learns to find his own courage. The crew regroups and battles the Trump siblings: Zoro defeats the swordsman Pin Joker, Sanji overcomes Boo Jack, Usopp takes down Skunk One, and Nami traps Honey Queen in a bottle. Luffy faces Bear King, whose body can harden like steel. When the villain mocks Akisu for shielding Borodo, Luffy rebounds the blast of his giant cannon back at him, and Bear King falls as the island collapses into the sea. Akisu is reunited with his parents but chooses to continue thieving with Borodo.

The film earned about three billion yen, a record for the series until One Piece Film: Strong World in 2009. Its theme song, "Believe", was performed by Folder5.

Bumblebee's account begins on Cybertron, where the AllSpark, the source of all Transformer life, once allowed the planet to flourish under the joint leadership of Optimus Prime and Megatron. Megatron, however, becomes corrupted and tries to seize the artifact for himself, igniting the war between the Autobots and the Decepticons. Bumblebee fights to protect it, and the Autobots finally launch the AllSpark into space to keep it from Megatron, who destroys Bumblebee's voice before setting off in pursuit. Megatron tracks the cube to prehistoric Earth but becomes trapped in Arctic ice. Some four million years later, an expedition led by Captain Archibald Witwicky stumbles upon the frozen robot; Witwicky ends his days in a mental institution after filling page after page with alien designs, which draw the attention of the secret government agency Sector Seven. The agency excavates Megatron, discovers the AllSpark in Colorado and, decades later, oversees the building of the Hoover Dam. The story then jumps to 2003, when Bumblebee's arrival on Earth is detected and Sector Seven, led by Simmons, begins hunting the robot disguised as a yellow Camaro, while Sam Witwicky learns of his great-great-grandfather's legacy.

The short was not sold on its own: it was included on a bonus disc available only with the Walmart edition of the Transformers DVD, released in North America on 16 October 2007. The Transformers DVD itself became the fastest-selling DVD of 2007 in North America, with 8.3 million copies sold in its first week.

Denise Dupree (Naughton), a classically trained pianist with strict parents, secretly longs to sing, and Malik Washburn (Pennie), an aspiring actor and rapper, hides his enrollment from his overworked mother and refuses to talk in drama class about the death of his sister. When Malik overhears Denise singing, he and the musician Victor Tavares (Perez) persuade her to record with them, and a record executive later tells them that her voice is what interests him. The shy actress Jenny Garrison (Panabaker) begins a romance with the singer Marco Ramonte (Book), which is shaken when she meets a former student who promises to introduce her to his agent.

Other students face harder lessons. Joy Moy (Perez de Tagle) lands a role on Sesame Street but eventually drops out as her grades suffer, while the aspiring filmmaker Neil Baczynsky (Iacono) is swindled out of five thousand dollars by a supposed producer. In senior year the dancer Kevin Barrett (McGill) is told by Ms. Kraft (Neuwirth) that he lacks the talent to dance professionally and, devastated, tries to throw himself in front of a subway train before his friends stop him; he later resolves to go home and become a dance teacher. Denise defies her father by performing at a club concert, winning over her mother, and Jenny and Marco reconcile before the class comes together for the graduation performance of "Hold Your Dream".

The programme asks what drives a man who, after suffering a devastating tragedy, devotes his whole life to a single ideal, and what happens when one person takes it upon himself to fight a city's criminal underworld alone. It traces Bruce Wayne back to the formative trauma of witnessing his parents' murder as a child and examines how that loss shaped him, how he channels fear and grief into a disciplined double life, and how a boy scarred by violence turns himself into a symbol of hope for Gotham City. Along the way it weighs the appeal and the dangers of vigilante justice, and looks at the costumed villains of Batman's rogues' gallery as reflections of the hero's own psyche, including foes who had not appeared in the Nolan films.

The film is built mainly around interviews, illustrated with dynamic treatments of comic book panels and covers and with clips from Batman Begins and The Dark Knight. Contributors include the clinical psychologist Robin S. Rosenberg, who discusses the effect of the Waynes' murder on their son, alongside DC Comics figures Paul Levitz and Dan DiDio and the veteran Batman writers and editors Denny O'Neil and Len Wein. Christopher Nolan and Christian Bale also appear, speaking about their interpretation of the character.

The documentary was later included as a high-definition special feature on the second disc of Warner Home Video's Blu-ray release of The Dark Knight in December 2008, where it was described as a look into the psyche of Bruce Wayne through real-world psychotherapy, and it reappeared in later Dark Knight Trilogy box sets. It holds a favourable user rating on IMDb, where one reviewer called it a thorough, credible and engaging examination of the character.

Blade: House of Chthon is the two-hour 2006 pilot of the American television series Blade: The Series, created by David S. Goyer for Spike TV and based on the Marvel Comics vampire hunter. Directed by Peter O'Fallon from a script by Goyer and Geoff Johns, it was later released on DVD as a standalone film. Rapper Sticky Fingaz, credited as Kirk "Sticky" Jones, takes over the role of Eric Brooks / Blade from Wesley Snipes, with Jill Wagner as Krista Starr, Neil Jackson as Marcus van Sciver, Jessica Gower as Chase and Nelson Lee as Shen.

Set after the events of the film Blade: Trinity (2004), the story follows Krista Starr, a soldier who comes home from service in Iraq to learn that her twin brother, Zack, has died in mysterious circumstances. Investigating, she discovers that Zack had become a "familiar", a human who serves a vampire in the hope of one day being rewarded with eternal life. Her search leads her to Marcus van Sciver, a powerful vampire and high-ranking member of the House of Chthon, who killed Zack, and to Blade, the half-vampire hunter who realizes that hacking and slashing alone is getting him nowhere and that he needs to understand the inner workings of vampire society. Smitten with Krista, Marcus turns her into a vampire by injecting her with his own blood. Blade then injects her with the serum he uses to control his own thirst, prepared by his weaponsmith and hacker ally, Shen, and offers her the chance to avenge her brother by helping him bring down Marcus and his house. Revealing that Zack had been helping him with a sting operation, Blade forms a reluctant partnership with Krista, who must now maintain her cover inside the House of Chthon while battling her growing predatory instincts.

In this timeline, Goku dies of a viral heart disease, and because his death is from natural causes, he cannot be revived with the Dragon Balls. Six months later, two androids appear and kill Earth's greatest fighters, including Piccolo, Vegeta, Krillin, Tien and Yamcha. With Piccolo's death, Kami also dies and the Dragon Balls cease to exist, leaving no way to bring anyone back to life.

Thirteen years later, the androids have killed most of humanity and continue to terrorize the remaining survivors for sport. Gohan, Goku's son and the only surviving warrior, has become a Super Saiyan but still cannot defeat them. He trains Trunks, the teenage son of Vegeta and Bulma, who longs to reach the Super Saiyan level himself. After a battle in which Gohan loses an arm, he knocks Trunks unconscious and goes to face the androids alone, fearing that Earth would be left without a defender if both of them died. When Trunks finds Gohan's body, his grief and rage finally transform him into a Super Saiyan. Years later, after failing to defeat the androids alone, Trunks travels back in time in a machine built by his mother to bring Goku a cure for his heart disease, setting up the events of the main series.

The special is known for its dark, tragic tone, which contrasts with much of the series, and for its focus on the bond between Gohan and Trunks.

In North America, the special was released on VHS and DVD in October 2000 by Funimation and later as a remastered double feature with Bardock – The Father of Goku. Anime News Network praised its sympathetic characters and exceptional action sequences, while noting that familiarity with the television series is recommended.

Ryo Kawase (Ōno) is a reporter for a small magazine who writes about organized crime. His modest income is enough to rent a small apartment with a tiny bathtub and, unfortunately, an extremely thin wall, through which he can hear almost everything that happens next door. His neighbor is the beautiful Satsuki (Aoi), and Ryo soon becomes captivated by the sounds coming from her home: her bubble baths, her lovemaking with her boyfriend Yuta (Katō), and the obscene, frightening phone calls she receives at night. Methodical rather than desperate, he installs a movable microphone along the wall to hear more clearly, and even tells a co-worker casually about what he is doing, while imagining the scenes that go with the sounds. When he and Satsuki eventually meet, their series of platonic dates develops into a sweet friendship. A blind spot in his listening setup, however, leads him to discover that someone else has already bugged her apartment, and Ryo sets out to identify the intruder without revealing what he knows. When Satsuki at last wants to give herself to him, his desire fades: the real woman cannot match the one he has built in his imagination.

The film was released on DVD in the United States by TLA Releasing. Jeffrey M. Anderson of Combustible Celluloid gave it three stars out of four, likening it to an old-fashioned "nudie cutie" but finding it cheerful and spirited, praising Aoi's appeal and the fact that she is given a real role, and noting the director's use of sound, color and the Japanese cityscape, though he found the DVD transfer poor. The Swiss site Molodezhnaja considered it mediocre overall, finding the story thin and the voyeurism theme quickly exhausted, but singled out the ending as its most intelligent part.

While salvaging a wrecked pirate ship, the Straw Hat Pirates open a treasure chest and find an old woman, Roba, hiding inside. In exchange for a ride home to Mecha Island, she tells them of a legendary golden crown that only the king of the sea may wear. As they approach, an old folk song drifts across the water, and the island's defence machines open fire. The island's lord is Roba's son, Dr. Ratchet, a gaunt, highly strung young inventor with a lifelong dream of world domination, who had been trying in vain to decipher the song's riddle. When he sees that Luffy and his crew have already begun to crack it by instinct, he invites them to his castle and proposes they search together.

Guided by the song, the group enters a cave beneath the island and, after solving a series of puzzles, discovers that Mecha Island is actually the back of a gigantic turtle. Ratchet reveals that this was his goal all along: from his castle he binds the creature with cables, intending to use it to conquer the world. The turtle tells Chopper that it wakes only once every thousand years to lay its eggs, and cannot do so while restrained. The Straw Hats battle Ratchet's bumbling henchmen, General Maji and Colonel Honki, and their machines, while Luffy faces the inventor's series of fighting robots, ending with a giant mechanical tortoise. Discovering Gear Second by accident for the first time, Luffy defeats Ratchet and wrecks the castle, freeing the turtle, and the crew learns that the golden treasure is in fact the shell of its eggs.

The regular voice cast includes Mayumi Tanaka as Luffy, Kazuya Nakai as Zoro, Akemi Okamura as Nami, Kappei Yamaguchi as Usopp, Hiroaki Hirata as Sanji, Yuriko Yamaguchi as Robin and Kazue Ikura standing in as Chopper. Gorō Inagaki makes a special guest appearance as Ratchet, with Takeshi Aono as the family butler, and the theme song "Sayaendō" is performed by NEWS. The film was later released on DVD in Germany and France.

The film is set in an alternate continuity: the crew has already traveled beyond Enies Lobby, sails the Thousand Sunny and includes Nico Robin and Franky, yet still has no ship's doctor, while Vivi and Karoo are absent. When Nami falls gravely ill, the crew lands on the snowbound Drum Kingdom, where the only remaining doctor is Dr. Kureha, who lives in the castle atop a mountain. Luffy carries Nami up the peak and reaches the top half-frozen, and Kureha treats them with the help of her assistant Chopper, a talking reindeer shunned by his own kind for his blue nose and feared by humans after he ate the Human-Human Fruit. The tyrannical King Wapol, who controlled his people by hoarding all the doctors and fled when Blackbeard's pirates attacked, now returns with his older brother Musshuru, a poison-mushroom user exiled after unleashing deadly spores on the kingdom years earlier.

Flashbacks recount how Chopper was inspired to become a doctor by the eccentric quack Hiriluk, whose death he blames on himself. Musshuru nearly kills Luffy with his spores, but an antidote saves him, and with the help of his crewmates and Chopper, Luffy defeats the brothers using his Gear techniques. Chopper accepts Luffy's invitation to become the crew's doctor, and as the Straw Hats depart, Kureha fires Hiriluk's special powder into the sky, turning the falling snow into a vision of pink cherry blossoms.

Each part opens with narration over biblical images telling the legend of the fallen angels and of the Nephilim, half-angel, half-human beings considered abominations, whom soldier angels known as the Powers are determined to purge from the world. Aaron is a troubled orphan who has spent three years with a loving foster family in a small American town. He has become a popular wrestling star at school and has learned to control the violent urges that plagued his past. On his eighteenth birthday, however, he begins to suffer intense headaches, discovers he can understand and speak languages he has never studied, displays sudden bursts of strength and is alarmed to hear the thoughts of his dog Gabriel, all of which disrupts his studies and his budding romance with his classmate Vilma. A homeless man named Zeke, actually a fallen angel in disguise, reveals that Aaron is a Nephilim and that few like him survive the transformation. Aaron also learns that he may be the Redeemer of prophecy, able to absolve fallen angels and send them back to Heaven, which puts him in the sights of the Powers, led by the ruthless Verchiel, who hunt him down.

The two later parts, The Journey and The Destiny, aired in 2007, bringing the full miniseries to over four hours. In Variety, Laura Fries noted that the film follows the books closely in plot, though Verchiel, male in the novels, is played by a woman. She found Cooper's script talky and its symbolism simplistic, and Salomon's camera gimmicks distracting, but credited the film with deeper character development than expected and decent effects. Reviewing the miniseries on DVD Talk, Thomas Spurlin praised Wesley's performance and the supporting cast but found the exposition-heavy story far too long.

The short takes place in the Candy Apple, the friendly new incarnation of the Poison Apple tavern, where Donkey hosts a Christmas party and persuades everyone to join him in a caroling stage show. He opens with "It's the Most Wonderful Time of the Year" alongside his fairy-tale friends. Shrek, who surprises everyone by agreeing to sing, joins Fiona, their three ogre children and the ogre army in a gleefully gross ogre version of "Jingle Bells", with lyrics about bug cocoons and cricket slurps. Puss in Boots follows with "Fleas Navidad", a take on "Feliz Navidad" that he claims is a classic from his village, and the whole company closes with "Fairy Tale Rock", a rendition of "Jingle Bell Rock". Running gags in the background include Gingy trying to rescue lifeless gingerbread cookies, the Three Little Pigs preparing for swimsuit weather and Rumpelstiltskin trapped in a cage.

Eddie Murphy returns as Donkey, after being replaced by Dean Edwards in Scared Shrekless, alongside Mike Myers as Shrek, Cameron Diaz as Fiona and Antonio Banderas as Puss. Walt Dohrn voices Rumpelstiltskin, Jon Hamm the ogre Brogan, Cody Cameron Pinocchio and the pigs, Conrad Vernon Gingy and Aron Warner the Big Bad Wolf, with Craig Robinson and Jane Lynch also among the ogres. It was the last Shrek production to reunite the core original cast until Shrek 5.

The holiday disc rounds out the main short with a Donkey decoration game and Shrek's Yule Log, a half-hour virtual fireplace in Shrek's house in which characters such as Rumpelstiltskin, Puss, Fiona and Gingy wander through with festive gags.

Top-secret government experiments in teleportation and time travel have been shut down as too dangerous, and their lead scientist, Winter, has disappeared with the technology, a portable teleporter that opens a wormhole through space and time and had previously been tested only on small animals such as mice. A passenger jet crashes in the American Midwest with no survivors, yet investigators discover that the aircraft, Flight 507 to Mexico, is not due to depart until the following day: it has apparently travelled into the past. When Winter's name turns up on the flight's manifest, the government orders the plane turned back and, to protect the project, the President authorises fighter jets to shoot it down, despite the pleas of Caleb, whose wife Claire and daughter Sarah are on board for a holiday.

At the last moment Winter activates the device by remote control and the plane vanishes into another dimension; only the passengers closest to the teleporter survive the jump. Aboard, the corrupt agent David Martin and his accomplice Liam take the survivors hostage and try to force Winter to send the aircraft back to coordinates of their choosing. On the ground, Caleb tracks down Winter's girlfriend and recovers a second remote hidden in her house, while the open wormhole spawns a swelling vortex in the sky whose lightning makes helicopters, buildings and people disappear, and which scientists warn will destroy the universe unless it is closed. Sarah restores the failing teleporter's power, and Caleb opens a wormhole of his own to reach the plane. In the ensuing struggle Claire is killed, Liam is struck by the lightning and Martin is thrown from the fuselage, before Caleb sends the plane back to the moment before Flight 507 took off. Forewarned by a photograph he sends to his own phone, he has Winter and the two conspirators arrested before departure.

The cast also includes Stefanie von Pfetten as Claire, Ashley Whillans as Sarah, Gary Hudson as Martin, Michael Eklund as Liam, Garwin Sanford and Erin Karpluk. The film premiered on German television on RTL II in March 2009.

The film opens with an extended account of the legend at its heart. Hidden in the mountains of the American Southwest is a secret pass leading to Natocchue, a spiritual paradise inhabited by benevolent spirits, where lost and abandoned animals can live in peace, away from the cruelty of the human world. The animals are led there by guardians, shamans chosen by the Spirit of the Wind and gifted with extraordinary powers; in every generation the spirit selects a new guardian and entrusts him with the key that opens the way through the pass. Manu lives in the desert mountains with his grandfather, Nitika and Nica, and spends his days racing, unaware of his family's heritage. He learns that the duty of guarding the animals has been handed down through his family and that the Spirit of the Wind has chosen him as the next guardian. Meanwhile a mismatched troop of animals, fleeing an ancient magic, crosses paths with Manu and Nica as the two children escape a strange whirlwind. Together with their family and these new animal companions, the young guardian must keep the key out of the hands of Calabar, Manu's uncle and a renegade former guardian who wants to seize the immense power of Natocchue for himself.

Discovered in 1994, the cave had been sealed for millennia by a rockfall at its entrance, preserving some 420 painted or engraved animal figures, as well as hand prints, animal bones and glittering mineral formations. The film moves slowly through the chambers, letting the camera dwell on the drawings while Herzog muses on what they reveal about the people who made them and about the origins of human imagination. Between these passages he interviews scientists and specialists connected with the site, among them Jean Clottes, Dominique Baffier and Jean-Michel Geneste, along with researchers such as Carole Fritz, Gilles Tosello, Julien Monney and Nicholas J. Conard. The film also visits the nearby Pont d'Arc natural bridge and the nuclear power station at Cruas, and ends with a dedication to Roger Ebert.

Access to Chauvet is tightly restricted. Herzog obtained special permission for six shooting days of four hours each, working with a crew of three, cinematographer Peter Zeitlinger, a sound recordist and an assistant, while lighting the scenes himself with cool, battery-powered lamps. The team had to stay on a narrow metal walkway, wear protective suits and limit their time inside because of high levels of carbon dioxide and radon. Initially sceptical of 3D, Herzog adopted it after visiting the cave, to capture how the painters used the bulges and contours of the rock. The score is by Ernst Reijseger.

In Maine, Bill drops Julia at the airport for her flight back to New York City, where she studies. Soon afterwards his colleague Dr. Divya, flying over Iceland, warns him that violent volcanic eruptions have broken loose an enormous mass of glacial ice hundreds of kilometers wide, which is now hurtling across the Atlantic toward North America; Divya is killed moments later. Bill picks up Teri at the office of the senator she works for, and the family sets out for New York to rescue Julia as the advancing ice brings a summer blizzard, closes airports and flattens Boston, while Air Force jets fail to break it apart.

The journey becomes a struggle for survival in temperatures of forty below. After crashing into an abandoned car, the Harts find a van, only to lose it to Gary, a desperate man heading for California who threatens them with a gun and later drowns when the van plunges through a frozen river. Sheltering in a house, they free Gerald, a man pinned beneath a fallen shelf, and in gratitude he lends them his light aircraft. Meanwhile Julia and her friend Logan try to escape the freezing city on foot through the subway and the Lincoln Tunnel. From the air the Harts witness a second failed attempt to stop the ice, then make an emergency landing when the plane leaks fuel. Tracking Julia's phone, they find her and Logan and take refuge at the Statue of Liberty, from where they watch the military finally destroy the glacier with a nuclear weapon, leaving New York buried in snow but saved.

Shot on a budget estimated at about $250,000 at The Asylum's Los Angeles studio and other locations including the Lacy Street Production Center and a movie ranch in Agua Dulce, the film premiered in the United States on 28 June 2011 and was later released direct to video in other countries, including France in 2012.

The film begins with the formation of the Earth and the emergence of life, then traces how human societies spread across continents and, especially in the past few decades, began to reshape the planet at unprecedented speed. Sweeping images of deserts, forests, ice caps, farmland and megacities illustrate its central themes: water shortages, deforestation, melting ice, the depletion of natural resources and the impact of human activity on climate change. Rather than presenting a disaster film, Arthus-Bertrand frames it as a message of hope, arguing that humanity still has roughly ten years to change course.

The shoot took about eighteen months, with the director, a cameraman, a camera engineer and a pilot flying a small helicopter over more than fifty countries on every continent, including Antarctica. Stabilized high-definition Cineflex cameras mounted beneath the helicopter gave the footage its smooth, crane-like quality, and nearly 500 hours of raw material were recorded. With a budget of about 12 million euros, largely funded by the PPR group (later Kering), Home was released on World Environment Day, 5 June 2009, simultaneously in cinemas, on television, on DVD and free on YouTube in 181 countries, and it was screened outdoors on the Champ de Mars in Paris. It drew more than 8 million viewers on France 2 and tens of millions of views online. Critics praised its imagery but questioned its preachy narration and the contrast between its message and its luxury-goods sponsor. It was nominated for the César Award for Best Documentary.

The story opens with Cobb recalling the lessons of his mentor Miles, who taught him the art of shared dreaming and insisted that creation should be for its own sake rather than for profit. Cobb, his point man Arthur and Nash, an unreliable architect chosen only because he was available, have been hired by Cobol Engineering to extract a secret from the mind of Mr. Kaneda, a paranoid executive. The dream takes the form of a downtown district of skyscrapers, a bank and an office tower, and Cobol insists on sending along several armed thugs as "tourists" to make sure the job gets done. Early on Cobb is distracted by a vision of his late wife Mal and is nearly killed by a bus, saved only by Arthur.

While Arthur and the tourists stage a jewellery-store robbery to draw off the police, Nash guides Cobb to Kaneda's office. Cobb threatens the executive and produces a bomb, but the dream begins to collapse after Nash is killed by Kaneda's receptionist. When Kaneda finally unlocks his computer, Cobb finds that the file he wants, the RDS-1 Energy Expansion Program, is protected by a password that only its originator, Saito, knows. The bomb goes off and Cobb wakes in a hostage room guarded by Cobol's men. The firm's chief, Woodruff, reveals that the information was meant to win Fischer Morrow's backing for an oil pipeline along Africa's eastern coast. Cobb agrees to go after Saito himself, on condition that there are no tourists and only he, Arthur and Nash take part, since Saito is trained in dream-sharing and will be on guard from the start. The prequel ends as Cobb prepares the plan that becomes the opening sequence of Inception.

The story picks up after the death of the detective L. High school prodigy turned college student Light Yagami, who has been secretly killing criminals as "Kira" with a supernatural notebook that kills anyone whose name is written in it, now leads the Japanese Kira investigation as the new L, while the shinigami Ryuk watches in amusement. Years later, with cults worshipping Kira, two young potential successors to L emerge: Near, who works with the United States government, and Mello, who obtains a Death Note of his own and turns it against Near's team; the hunt for Mello costs Light's father, Soichiro, his life. As suspicion falls once more on Misa Amane, Light passes her notebook to the fervent Kira supporter Teru Mikami and makes the newscaster Kiyomi Takada Kira's public spokesperson. Mello kidnaps Takada, who kills him before Light silences her. Near then arranges a meeting between Light and the remaining task force members, where Mikami tries to kill them all, but his notebook has been replaced with a decoy. Exposed as Kira and badly wounded, Light begs Ryuk for help, but the shinigami writes Light's name in his own notebook, as he had promised when they first met.

The film was broadcast by Nippon Television on 22 August 2008, nearly a year after the first Relight special. Like its predecessor, it reworks the material rather than simply replaying it, adding and omitting scenes; it contains more new footage than the first special and drops the mafia subplot, concentrating on the confrontation between Kira and L's successors Near and Mello. The original series, broadcast from October 2006 to June 2007, is widely acclaimed.

Charlotte appears to have a perfect life with Max, an attentive and handsome architect, and their young son Benjamin, to whom she reads the Brothers Grimm tale "The Girl Without Hands" at bedtime. Her marriage is affectionate and the couple's intimacy is warm and trusting. Yet she secretly rents a bare apartment where she meets men she picks from among her patients, most of them physically unprepossessing, for impulsive sexual encounters. When she unexpectedly runs into one of these men again and he tries to get close to her, she breaks down, attacks him and collapses.

Her affairs come to light, she is struck off the medical register and her marriage nearly falls apart. In couples therapy and a psychiatric assessment she struggles, or declines, to explain her behaviour, admitting she does not really know what she is supposed to feel. In the film's third section, two years later, the family has moved to India, where Max works as an architect; twins have been born and their happiness seems restored, but Max cannot shake his mistrust and begins following Charlotte on her solitary morning walks, which take her to a building under construction.

The documentary is divided into eleven chapters. It begins with the stalled early attempts at a sequel, Cameron's recruitment and the pay dispute that briefly threatened Weaver's return as Ripley, then moves to the design of the colony, the spaceships and the armored personnel carrier, and to the casting of the Colonial Marines and their military-style training. A chapter on the shoot at Pinewood Studios in 1985 details tensions between the American director and the British crew, including the replacement of the original cinematographer, and the late casting of Biehn. Further chapters examine the Marines' weapons and the action sequences, the redesigned facehuggers and warrior aliens, the bond between Weaver and the nine-year-old Henn, and the construction of the full-size Alien Queen puppet and the Power Loader for their climactic duel. The last chapters cover Horner's struggle to compose the score in very little time, which soured his relationship with Cameron for years, the miniature visual effects, and the film's reception, including Weaver's Academy Award nomination for Best Actress.

The documentary was later included in the Aliens collector's edition DVD and, in a reformatted widescreen version, in the Alien Anthology Blu-ray set, which added deleted segments known as enhancement pods.

Lorraine is a recently separated single mother with a low-paying job, struggling to make ends meet while raising her ten-year-old son. She buys gas a few dollars at a time, settles for frozen convenience-store snacks instead of pizza, attends group therapy sessions where she is encouraged to stand up for herself, and has to fend off her estranged husband, a soldier, who is seeking sole custody of Chad. One night, during a stop at a gas station, mother and son are carjacked by Roy, a charismatic bank robber on the run, who takes over the car and orders Lorraine to drive toward an uncertain destination, with no intention of letting them go. Much of the story unfolds inside the vehicle as the two adults trade barbs, alternate between moments of uneasy rapport and failed escape attempts, and engage in a power struggle over her and the boy's fate. Lorraine misses several chances to alert others, including at a police roadblock, and resorts to writing her license plate number and a plea for help in a diner restroom and to bouts of reckless driving. In the final stretch, the film turns into an action thriller, as Lorraine, who has finally had enough, takes up a shotgun and the chase ends in a massive pile-up.

Released on DVD in the United States in November 2011, Carjacked received largely negative reviews, with critics complaining that the promising premise and capable leads were wasted on a flat, implausible script. David Nusair of Reel Film Reviews gave it one star out of four, finding no menace or suspense, unconvincing dialogue and a heavy-handed self-empowerment subplot. Jason Rugaard of Movie Mavericks likened it to a lesser version of A Perfect World, praising Dorff's screen presence but faulting the static staging and a laughable script, with action arriving only after an hour. Jim McLennan of Film Blitz considered Bello and Dorff well cast and some of their conversations almost engaging, and enjoyed the outlandish climax, but wished the rest of the film had shared its energy.

On a Kansas farm, Aunt Em asks Tom and Jerry, here Dorothy Gale's pets alongside her dog Toto, to keep an eye on the girl. When a cyclone strikes, the pair are swept away to the Land of Oz and land on the yellow brick road. From Tuffy, a young Munchkin mouse, they learn that Dorothy and Toto have already set off for the Emerald City, and the three follow. Along the way they save Dorothy and her new companions, the Scarecrow, the Tin Man and the Cowardly Lion, from a rockslide engineered by the Wicked Witch of the West, and run into familiar faces such as Butch and Droopy.

The Wizard agrees to grant the travellers' wishes only if they bring him the Witch's broomstick. At her castle, the Witch's guards corner Dorothy and her friends and the Witch sets the Scarecrow on fire, but Tom, Jerry and Tuffy douse him with a bucket of water that also splashes the Witch, who melts away. When the Wizard then refuses to keep his promise, Jerry spots the man behind the curtain and, with Tom's help, exposes him. Back home in Kansas, no one believes Dorothy's story except Tom and Jerry, who confirm it.

Grey DeLisle voices Dorothy, with Nikki Yanofsky providing her singing voice; Joe Alaskey voices the Wizard, Butch and Droopy, Michael Gough the Scarecrow, Rob Paulsen the Tin Man, Todd Stashwick the Lion, Frances Conroy Aunt Em and Glinda, Laraine Newman the Wicked Witch, Stephen Root Uncle Henry and Kath Soucie Tuffy. Warner Home Video released it on DVD and Blu-ray on 23 August 2011. Common Sense Media gave it three stars out of five, and a sequel, Tom and Jerry: Back to Oz, followed in 2016.

Schneider, an aging pirate who senses that he does not have long to live, decides to disband his tiny crew, which consists only of himself and his old dog Buzz, in order to spare his companion. Buzz refuses to leave, so Schneider sets him an impossible challenge: if he can steal the straw hat of the famous pirate Monkey D. Luffy, the crew will stay together. Buzz, who ate a Devil Fruit that allows him to transform into a giant eagle, succeeds, snatching the treasured hat that Luffy received from Shanks. The Straw Hat Pirates, who had rescued Schneider from a drifting ship, set off in a long, frantic pursuit of the eagle, while Chopper tends to the ailing old man. The chase eventually leads Luffy and Buzz into a Navy base, where the crew fights its way through the Marines and wins. In the end Luffy recovers his hat, Schneider and Buzz befriend the Straw Hats, and the old pirate promises not to break up his crew. A closing flashback shows Shanks entrusting the hat to the young Luffy.

Six college friends head into the wilderness on a camping trip to blow off steam, only to find themselves the quarry of a monstrous alien that begins hunting them in a deadly game of cat and mouse. Unsure what they are facing or whom to trust, the group struggles to defend itself as the creature closes in. Help appears in the form of Ava, another, seemingly friendly alien who orbits the Earth and can reach them only by appearing in the form of an avatar. Reluctantly joining forces with her, the survivors learn that they have just one chance to stop the monster: they must find and repair the robot Ava has sent down to Earth before the creature slaughters them one by one.

The cast is led by Jason Lockhart as Tyler, Kim Argetsinger as Jesse and Cassie Fliegel as Ava, with Dylan Vox as Jake, Marlene Mc'Cohen as Tiffany, Ginny You as Dana and Georgina Tolentino as Crystal. The film was shot in Los Angeles in the summer of 2010, while Schoenbrun was finishing post-production on The Amazing Bulk; he considered it the harder production of the two because of its many shooting locations.

The film received no theatrical release and was issued directly to video, DVD and television on 20 September 2011, becoming Schoenbrun's most widely released film that year. Reviews were overwhelmingly negative. The horror blogger Baron Craze dismissed its dialogue as half-baked drivel and found it boring, and Richard Scheib called it only marginally better made than the kind of film teenagers shoot on a camcorder over successive weekends, though it found some fans on home video in Japan. In 2012 Tom Cat Films sued hundreds of anonymous "John Doe" defendants in U.S. federal court for allegedly downloading the film illegally, a suit that commentators described as copyright trolling.

Raised by Doris, a free-spirited therapist of the 1968 generation, Lena has become her opposite: controlled, rule-bound and wary of emotion. For her graduation, mother and daughter fly to Thailand, sitting next to the Öztürks, a widowed police detective, Metin, and his children, the macho would-be rapper Cem and his sister Yağmur. When an ash cloud forces the plane to ditch in the Indian Ocean, most passengers are rescued, but Lena drifts ashore on a deserted island in a life raft with Cem, Yağmur and Costa, a stuttering Greek. Their radio contact with their parents reveals that the raft's beacon is too weak to be located.

As the castaways struggle to get by, Lena and Cem constantly clash. After Lena steps on a sea urchin and suffers an allergic reaction, Cem carries her to a village of supposed cannibals, who turn out to speak fluent German and are hosting a researcher who treats her. At a celebration, Lena believes she slept with Cem while intoxicated and later overhears that he had made a bet about it. Meanwhile, Doris and Metin fall in love at the resort. Once reunited with her mother, the hurt Lena drives the Öztürks away by making Metin believe that the mafia clan that put the family in witness protection has found them. When she later watches her camcorder footage and sees that Cem only watched over her while she slept, she confesses everything. She and Doris catch up with the Öztürks on the plane as they leave with new identities, and both couples are reunited.

Shot over 37 days in 2011 in Munich, Berlin and Thailand, whose islands Ko Kut and Ko Chang stood in for the Andaman Islands, the film premiered in Munich on 6 March 2012 and opened in German cinemas on 15 March 2012.

The story is set on the low-budget shoot of an adult film. As production gets under way, a mysterious, sexually transmitted infection begins spreading through the cast, turning the performers one after another into rabid, flesh-eating zombies who turn on their colleagues. The remaining cast and crew members, trapped together on the job, must work out what is causing their fellow stars to attack them and find a way to survive before they too are infected or devoured. Despite the title and the setting, the film contains relatively little sexual content, drawing most of its humour from dirty jokes, innuendo and the banter of its characters.

The cast includes Joshua Cameron as Gavin, alongside Alicia Oberle, Kevin Cazier, Kira Ratterman and Vivi Wreen. The gore effects were made cheaply, with one reviewer suspecting chocolate syrup and spare meat.

After its completion the film was marketed for distribution with a brief theatrical run and some exposure around the 2012 Cannes Film Festival, and it was then released on DVD by R-Squared Films. Reviews were limited and mixed. ML Miller compared it less to David Cronenberg's early sexually transmitted horror films Shivers and Rabid than to Kevin Smith's Clerks, citing its monochrome photography, sometimes witty dialogue and amateur performances. He felt the dialogue often sounded like actors reading someone else's distinctive writing rather than natural conversation and that it was more comedy than horror, but found it frequently funny, credited Emerson with getting a lot out of very little and concluded that it was worth a few laughs. Other reviewers and viewers were less forgiving, describing it as crude and amateurish, with weak acting and effects.

The film follows the lives of four former adult film performers - Rick, Tera, Jayden, and Georgette - as they navigate their post-porn careers. The movie explores the harsh realities of life after leaving the adult entertainment industry, including financial struggles, relationship issues, and personal crises.

At the beginning of the film, we see each performer struggling to cope with the transition from a lucrative career in adult films to an uncertain future. Rick, who was one of the most popular performers before retiring, is now working as a janitor and dealing with depression. Tera, on the other hand, has started her own business but struggles to make ends meet.

As the film progresses, we see each performer facing unique challenges. Jayden, who had been struggling with addiction, begins to rebuild his life and find new purpose. Georgette, who had become a successful entrepreneur, faces financial difficulties due to the instability of her business.

Throughout the film, Breitenbach raises questions about the exploitation of adult performers and the lack of support systems in place for those leaving the industry. He also highlights the importance of mental health awareness and the need for resources to help former performers transition to new careers.

The film's title, After Porn Ends, is a poignant commentary on the fleeting nature of fame and fortune in the adult entertainment industry. The movie serves as a warning to young performers about the potential consequences of entering this field without proper support or planning.

Ultimately, the film offers a nuanced portrayal of life after porn, highlighting both the difficulties and the resilience of former performers. By sharing their stories, the performers hope to raise awareness about the need for better support systems and resources for those leaving the industry.

The ending of the film is bittersweet, with each performer reflecting on their experiences and the lessons they've learned. While some have found success in new careers, others continue to struggle, serving as a reminder that life after porn can be complex and challenging.

The movie begins with Ash Ketchum, a young Pokémon trainer from Pallet Town, who has been searching for the mythical Pokémon Victini. According to legend, Victini can grant wishes to those who possess it. Ash is determined to find Victini before his rival, Barry, does.

Ash and his friends, Iris and Cilan, arrive in Elesa's city, where they meet Elesa, a powerful Electric-type Pokémon trainer from Unova. Elesa has been searching for Reshiram, the mythical Pokémon said to have the power to control time. Ash and his friends soon discover that Reshiram is being held captive by Team Plasma, a group of rogue trainers who seek to free all Pokémon from their trainers.

As Ash and his friends try to rescue Reshiram, they learn about the history of Reshiram and its connection to the mythical Pokémon Victini. According to legend, Reshiram and Victini were once connected, but they were separated by a powerful artifact known as the "Reshiram Crystal." The crystal was said to have been created by the ancient Pokémon, Dialga.

Ash and his friends soon discover that Team Plasma is planning to use the Reshiram Crystal to free all Pokémon from their trainers. They also learn that Elesa's city is in danger of being destroyed if the crystal is used.

The movie takes a dramatic turn when Ash and his friends are forced to make a difficult choice: to save Elesa's city or to rescue Reshiram. In the end, they decide to work together with Team Plasma to stop the destruction of the city.

In the climactic final battle, Ash and his friends face off against Team Plasma leader, Ghetsis. With the help of Elesa and her Pokémon, Ash is able to defeat Ghetsis and shatter the Reshiram Crystal, freeing Reshiram from its prison.

With Reshiram freed, it is revealed that the crystal was actually a powerful artifact created by Dialga, which had been keeping Reshiram captive for centuries. The movie ends with Ash and his friends reflecting on their adventure and the lessons they learned about friendship and teamwork.

Overall, Pokémon the Movie: Black - Victini and Reshiram is an action-packed adventure that explores themes of friendship, teamwork, and the importance of understanding and respecting the natural world.

A prologue set years earlier shows a woman drowning her two children in a small river. Her horrified husband confronts her, calling her mad, and in the ensuing struggle she weeps over what she has done and kills herself with his knife; he carries her body away and hides it, and no one knows where it was left. In the present, six American students on a road trip to Mexico become stranded in a small town where that tragedy once took place. With nowhere else to stay, they accept the only lodging available, a small cabin, where inexplicable things begin to happen at night: the sound of a woman sobbing echoes through the house, and their growing fear keeps them trapped inside.

Soon they begin to glimpse a woman with a bloodied face who picks off whoever lets their guard down. Julie and Andrew find a rosary that seems to have belonged to the dead woman and search the house, only to hear the ghost crying out for her children as they piece together the truth behind the legend. In the end La Llorona kills all of the friends except Julie, who is possessed by the spirit and murders the man who looks after the cabin before disappearing.

The cast is led by Vanessa Rice as Julie and John Patrick Jordan as Andrew, with Brenda Mejia as Ashley, Eltony Williams as Jay, Nicole Danielle as Michelle and Hugo Medina as Mike. The film was followed by a sequel, The Wailer 2 (2007), in which a professor searches Mexico for his missing daughter Julie, and by a prequel, The Wailer 3 (2012), set before the events of the first two films. Critical response from the horror blogs that reviewed it was largely negative, faulting its clichés, slow pacing, weak acting and reliance on cheap jump scares, though a few reviewers singled out the design of the ghost and some effective moments; the Fringes of Horror blog gave it its lowest rating.

The story continues the war between the Kingdom of Midland and the Tudor Empire, in which Griffith's mercenary company, the Band of the Hawk, has become one of Midland's most valuable forces. After Guts and Casca are separated from the rest of the band, they are pursued by the brutal Tudor commander Adon and his soldiers. Guts holds off most of the attackers so that Casca can escape, and in the aftermath he reflects on his life and resolves that one day he will leave the Hawks, find a dream of his own and so become Griffith's equal and true friend, rather than a follower serving someone else's ambition.

The band then takes part in the assault on Doldrey, a fortress thought to be impregnable, whose capture would bring the Hundred Years' War to an end. In the battle Casca kills Adon, and the long war finally comes to an end. A month after the war ends, however, Guts announces his departure and defeats Griffith in a duel to win his freedom. Shaken by the loss, Griffith makes a reckless mistake: he is discovered sleeping with the king's daughter, Princess Charlotte. He is charged with treason and thrown into the Tower of Rebirth, while the members of the Band of the Hawk are declared outlaws, setting up the events of the final film.

The film opened in Japan on 23 June 2012 and was released on home video in North America by Viz Media in 2013. Its producer reports that it was nominated in the feature film category at the 2013 Annecy International Animated Film Festival. Critical reaction was mixed. Kotaku's Richard Eisenbeis called it a great improvement over the first film, and Otaku USA praised its balance of action and character development. Anime News Network reviewers, by contrast, criticised its computer-generated animation and its treatment of women, and felt that it reduced the rich character development of the manga to a thin shadow.

The movie takes place during the Saiyan Saga of the Dragon Ball series and serves as a prequel to the original Dragon Ball Z series. The story revolves around Bardock, the father of Goku, who is a powerful Saiyan warrior.

The film begins with Bardock's life on Planet Vegeta, where he lives alongside his wife, Gine, and their son, Kakarot (Goku). However, Bardock is not happy with his life on Vegeta due to its strict rules and the constant threat of war. He longs for a more peaceful existence.

One day, Bardock discovers that Planet Vegeta is facing an impending attack by Frieza, a powerful and ruthless Saiyan warrior who seeks to conquer and destroy all other planets in the universe. The Saiyans are ordered to prepare for battle, but Bardock refuses to fight, citing his desire for peace and his love for his family.

As the war between Vegeta and Frieza begins, Bardock's actions become increasingly reckless, causing tension among the Saiyan warriors. In a final confrontation with Frieza, Bardock is killed by the villainous warrior.

The film then jumps forward in time to show Goku as a young boy on Earth, where he meets his future wife, Chi-Chi, and begins his training under Master Roshi. The movie ends with Goku's determination to become strong enough to surpass his father's legacy and protect those he cares about.

Throughout the film, Bardock's character is explored in depth, revealing his complexities and motivations. His desire for peace and family ultimately lead to his downfall, but also serve as a catalyst for Goku's growth and development as a warrior.

Overall, Dragon Ball: Episode of Bardock provides valuable insight into the backstory of the Dragon Ball Z series and offers a unique perspective on the character of Bardock.

The story begins with Bruce Wayne, now an older and retired Batman, who lives a quiet life as a wealthy businessman. However, when he witnesses a group of thugs beating up a young woman, his instincts kick in, and he returns to his crime-fighting roots. He dons the iconic Batsuit once again and sets out to reclaim Gotham City from the forces of evil.

The main antagonist is a corrupt and violent police commissioner, James Gordon Jr., who has become a puppet for the villainous Marv, a brutal and sadistic killer. The Joker, also known as Jack Napier, has escaped from Arkham Asylum and is wreaking havoc on Gotham City. He is determined to destroy Batman and prove that he is still the most unpredictable and deadly force in the city.

As Batman delves deeper into the world of crime, he must confront his own mortality and the consequences of his actions. He also faces a new generation of villains, including the Riddler, Two-Face, and the Mutants, who are terrorizing the city.

Meanwhile, Bruce Wayne's relationship with his daughter, Selina Kyle (later known as Catwoman), is explored in depth. She is a skilled thief and acrobat who becomes embroiled in her father's crusade against crime. The two form an uneasy alliance, with Selina often walking the fine line between helping Batman and pursuing her own interests.

Throughout the movie, Miller's signature dark and gritty style is evident, as he explores themes of decay, corruption, and the blurred lines between heroism and villainy. The animation is stunning, with a muted color palette that adds to the overall sense of unease and foreboding.

The film ends on a cliffhanger, setting up Part 2 for the next installment in the series. Batman's battle against the Joker reaches its climax, but the outcome is far from certain. Will he emerge victorious, or will the Clown Prince of Crime prove to be his undoing?

Overall, Batman: The Dark Knight Returns, Part 1 is a gripping and thought-provoking adaptation that stays true to Miller's original vision. It is a must-see for fans of the comic book series and anyone who loves a good superhero story.

Ash, Brock, May and Max are invited to the laboratory of the scientist Dr. Yung, where they are reunited with Misty and Professor Oak, who have also been invited. Yung demonstrates his Mirage System, a machine that can project extremely powerful artificial Pokémon able to move and fight anywhere within its range, and a Mirage Pokémon easily defeats Misty's Staryu. Pikachu notices the legendary Mew hiding nearby. Suddenly a masked figure calling himself the Mirage Master seizes control of the system, abducts Yung and Oak, and drives the others out with an army of Mirage Pokémon.

The Mirage Master demands Oak's password to his research data, intending to combine it with the system to create the ultimate Pokémon. Mew tries to help but is overpowered. Ash and Misty sneak back into the lab through an underground waterway, only to be ambushed; Team Rocket, who are trying to steal the invention, are sent flying, Pikachu is captured, and the pair are left for dead. Mew revives Ash and reveals that it too is a Mirage Pokémon, while May rescues Misty. By tormenting Pikachu, the villain forces Oak to give up the password and creates a Mirage Mewtwo that knows every move, wiping out the other mirages and easily beating Oak's Dragonite. He then extends the system's reach worldwide, and Oak unmasks him as Yung himself. When Mewtwo is about to finish off Pikachu, Mew sacrifices itself to hold it in place, letting Pikachu destroy it with its strongest attack. The system collapses, and the defeated Yung disappears as his laboratory crumbles around him.

Outside the Radiator Springs courthouse, Lizzie greets Lightning McQueen and Mater curtly but speaks fondly to the statue of the town's founder, Stanley, prompting McQueen to ask how the two met. Mater explains that it all started the week before, when a new town sign with a clock fell on him, leaving the clock on his nose; when he sneezed, he vanished and found himself in the Tail Light Caverns in 1909, before the town existed. At a nearby spring he meets a young Stanley, a radiator cap salesman about to leave for California in search of customers. Realising that without Stanley there will be no Radiator Springs, Mater zips back to the present to fetch McQueen, removes his radiator cap so that Stanley has a customer, and suggests he build a town beside "this here radiator spring". Stanley loves the idea and names the town on the spot.

Jumping ahead to 1927, the pair find the young town thriving when a Model T named Lizzie breaks down there. Mater fears she is falling for McQueen, which would ruin history, but it turns out she only has eyes for Stanley. McQueen introduces them, and the friends later return in time to see the couple marry before honeymooning at Comfy Caverns. Back in the present, McQueen insists that time travel is impossible, until Lizzie thanks him for introducing her to Stanley.

Larry the Cable Guy voices Mater, Keith Ferguson Lightning McQueen, John Michael Higgins Stanley and Katherine Helmond Lizzie. Unusually for the series, McQueen appears in his World Grand Prix paint scheme from Cars 2, the twins Mia and Tia do not appear, and each era is given its own colour treatment reminiscent of photographs from the period. Several locations seen in the short, including the caverns, are drawn from the Cars Land attraction.

Having crushed the Mutant gang's reign of terror, the returning Batman now faces two final confrontations. The Joker, feigning remorse, persuades his psychiatrist Dr. Wolper to bring him on a television talk show to tell his story, while a henchman supplies him with a mind-controlling lipstick. Meanwhile, Superman, who works as a government agent in exchange for permission to help people in secret, is asked by the President to put an end to Batman's vigilantism, against the backdrop of rising tension between the United States and the Soviet Union over the island of Corto Maltese. Gordon's successor, Commissioner Yindel, orders Batman's arrest. On the talk show, the Joker kills the entire studio audience with his laughing gas and escapes, then uses an aging Selina Kyle's escort service to take control of a congressman. Batman pursues him to a county fair, where the Joker kills dozens of people; in their brutal fight Batman breaks his neck without finishing him, and the Joker, stabbing the hero repeatedly, completes the job himself to frame Batman for murder. After Superman deflects a Soviet nuclear missile, the electromagnetic pulse plunges the country into darkness, and Batman rallies the Sons of Batman and Gotham's citizens to keep order. Ordered to stop him, Superman confronts Batman in Crime Alley, where the old hero, wearing a powered exoskeleton and helped by the one-armed Oliver Queen's kryptonite arrow, defeats him before apparently dying of a heart attack. At the funeral, Superman hears a faint heartbeat and winks at Carrie, and Bruce is later revealed to have faked his death to continue his mission in secret with Carrie, Queen and his followers.

The film was released on home video in January 2013, following Part 1 in 2012. Christopher Drake's music for both parts was released by WaterTower Music in October 2013.

A year has passed since Guts left the mercenary company known as the Band of the Hawk to pursue his own dream. In his absence, Griffith was caught in a liaison with the king's daughter, Princess Charlotte, imprisoned for treason in the Tower of Rebirth and tortured, while his followers were branded outlaws and hunted. Guts rejoins his old comrades to rescue him, but the man they free from the dungeon is a broken, mute and withered figure, barely alive after months of torture.

Overwhelmed by despair, Griffith tries to kill himself, and the strange pendant he has always worn reacts to his anguish. It opens a gateway to another realm under a solar eclipse, pulling Griffith and the entire Band of the Hawk inside. There they face the God Hand, a circle of archdemons, who tell Griffith that his whole life has been leading to this moment. He agrees to sacrifice his comrades in return for rebirth as Femto, a new member of the God Hand. The Hawks are massacred by monstrous Apostles, former humans like the demon Zodd, and Femto assaults Casca while Guts, fighting desperately to reach her, loses his left arm and his right eye. The mysterious Skull Knight carries Guts and the shattered Casca back to the human world and warns Guts that he now bears a brand that will draw evil spirits to him every night. Leaving Casca in the care of their former comrade Rickert, Guts sets out to hunt the Apostles and the God Hand.

At Flo's V8 Café, Lightning McQueen and Mater watch a monster truck roll by, and Mater scoffs that he used to wrestle trucks far bigger than that. He then launches into an outlandish account of his past, this time as a professional monster truck wrestler. In 1975 he starts out in a small-time ring, introduced by the announcer as "The Tormentor", to the boos of the crowd. His first opponent is the I-Screamer, a monstrous ice cream truck; Mater flees, then returns disguised as a kid in a propeller hat, orders a sundae and, while his rival's back is turned, hooks him and flips him onto his roof to win.

With a new look and a bigger set of wheels, The Tormentor works his way up the ranks, pinning Captain Collision, overturning the Rasta Carian by snatching away his bungee-cord dreadlocks, launching Dr. Feel Bad out of the ring and into hospital, and leaving Paddy O'Concrete covered in his own cement. At the world championship he expects an easy win over the reigning champion, Dr. Frankenwagon, until the doctor's enormous monster comes to life. When McQueen asks what happened next, Mater insists that the two of them fought as a tag team, and McQueen is pulled into the story in wrestling gear. After the monster turns on him, Mater hooks the creature, drives under the ring and pulls the whole thing over, defeating the doctor and his monster; the referee declares The Tormentor and "Frightening McMean" the new champions.

McQueen dismisses the tale as nonsense until The Tormentor's biggest fan arrives asking for Mater's autograph, and an eager McQueen's offer of his own leaves the fan uncomfortable. Larry the Cable Guy voices Mater and Keith Ferguson McQueen, with Jess Harnell as Captain Collision, Jan Rabson as the I-Screamer, Simon Petrie as the Rasta Carian, James Rankin as Dr. Feel Bad, Danny Mann as the referee, Lance Henriksen as Paddy O'Concrete and Frank Welker as the monster. Uploaded to Disney Junior's YouTube channel in 2024, it drew about five million views.

The movie revolves around a woman named Samantha, who returns to her hometown for Christmas after a painful breakup. She reconnects with her high school sweetheart, now a single father, and together they navigate their feelings amidst the festive atmosphere of the holiday season.

At its core, Love at the Christmas Table explores themes of second chances, forgiveness, and the power of love to heal emotional wounds. The film also touches on the idea that sometimes, people need time and space to work through their issues before they can truly move forward with their lives.

The movie's portrayal of Samantha's journey from heartbreak to healing is a poignant commentary on the human capacity for resilience and growth. As she navigates her feelings and reconnects with her past, she must also confront the challenges of co-parenting and rebuilding trust in a relationship.

Ultimately, Love at the Christmas Table is a feel-good holiday romance that celebrates the magic of love, forgiveness, and the transformative power of the holiday season.

Holden Price (Walker) comes home after his studies at Harvard and is surprised to discover that his father (Rekert), a wealthy, domineering and fiercely competitive man, has married Lana (Everhart), a woman much younger than himself. Their first meeting is an awkward one, as Holden walks in on her in the shower. Because his father is a workaholic who is seldom at home, Holden and Lana end up spending a great deal of time together, and he is soon drawn to her beauty and charisma. The two begin a passionate affair. When Holden learns that his hot-tempered father has been abusive toward Lana, he becomes visibly upset. Then his father is found dead, and both the son and his lover become suspects in the murder. The second half of the story turns into a whodunit built on a series of twists and double-crosses, in which the naive young man turns out to have been drawn into Lana's game.

The film drew middling notices. In The Great Canadian Guide to the Movies & TV, it received two and a half stars out of four and was described as a reasonably entertaining, noirish suspense drama with nice performances from Rekert and Everhart, though the reviewer felt the twists and double-crosses of its second half undermined the character drama established in the first. The Video Vacuum gave it two stars, finding the opening set-up solid and some of the romantic scenes effective, and crediting the chemistry between Everhart and Walker, who it said did a fine job as the naive son drawn into her game, but criticizing the dawdling pace of the second act and the telegraphed plot twists, and arguing that Hreno handled the seduction scenes better than the mystery and its tension.

Barbie plays Kristyn, a talented young ballerina in a ballet company who loves to get carried away by the music and improvise her own steps. Her strict teacher, Madame Natasha, demands absolute perfection and favours the company's star, Tara, who dances the solos opposite the handsome Dillon. When Natasha cuts Kristyn off during a rehearsal, she falls and breaks a slipper. With her best friend Hailey, the company's costume designer, she visits Madame Katerina, who has no shoes left in her size but, hearing Kristyn speak of her dream of dancing Giselle and Odette in Swan Lake, brings out a pair of sparkling pink shoes. As soon as Kristyn laces them up, she and Hailey are whisked away to a magical ballet world built from the stories whose costumes filled the room.

There Kristyn finally gets to dance the roles of her dreams, stepping into Giselle, a story of a young woman courted by both a prince and a woodsman, and Swan Lake, but the land is threatened by a cold and exacting Snow Queen, a reflection of Madame Natasha. To save her new friends and return home, Kristyn must defeat the queen through dance, realising that no step is wrong if it is danced from the heart. Back in the real world, she carries that lesson into a successful performance.
