Kelly Sheridan voices Kristyn and her ballet roles, with Katie Crown as Hailey, Ali Liebert as Tara and Odile, Brett Dier as Dillon and Prince Siegfried, Tabitha St. Germain as Madame Natasha and the Snow Queen, Lori Triolo as Madame Katerina, and Bill Mondy, Teryl Rothery, Trevor Devall and Kyle Rideout in supporting roles. The film weaves in music from classical ballets including La Laitière suisse, Adam's Giselle and Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake, alongside an original song by Dooley, Gabriel Mann and Rob Hudnut. It was followed by the streaming short Barbie in the Pink Shoes: Land of Sweets.

It Boy (20 ans d'écart) is a 2013 French romantic comedy co-written and directed by David Moreau, from an original idea by his co-writer Amro Hamzawi. Produced by Abel Nahmias for EuropaCorp with Echo Films, it stars Virginie Efira and Pierre Niney, with Charles Berling, Gilles Cohen, Amélie Glenn, Camille Japy, Michaël Abiteboul and Louis-Do de Lencquesaing in supporting roles.

Alice Lantins (Efira), 38, is a capable and ambitious journalist at the fashion magazine Rebelle and the obvious candidate to become its next editor-in-chief, except that her boss, Vincent Khan (Cohen), sees her as uptight and old-fashioned. Returning from a trip to Brazil, she sits next to Balthazar (Niney), an architecture student of about twenty who has landed in business class by chance. He finds a USB stick she dropped and, when she picks him up to retrieve it, he puts a helmet on her before giving her a ride on his pink scooter. Two colleagues snap a photo of the moment and post it online, and overnight Alice's image is transformed. Realizing that her boss suddenly sees her as daring, she decides to fake a romance with the younger man to secure the promotion.

Alice adopts a bolder style, visits Balthazar at university and goes out with him, and the pretense slowly turns into real feelings, leading to a passionate night together. Unable to tell him that she first approached him for her career, and afraid that he will one day find her too old, she breaks off the relationship, leaving him heartbroken while Vincent celebrates the "new Alice". When the head of the magazine group wants Balthazar for a photo shoot, he learns how Alice used him and confronts her in front of the whole team, and Vincent fires her for the deception. Alone, Alice revisits the places they shared and finally addresses Balthazar in a university lecture hall, admitting her mistakes and asking for a fresh start. They reunite, and she returns to her old dream of writing.

The documentary traces the long evolution of the project and Cameron's journey in bringing it to the screen, combining footage shot during development and production with archive material reaching back to 1995, before the making of Titanic. Cameron and producer Jon Landau recall and demonstrate their original tests of performance capture technology in that period, explain how the project was then set aside for about ten years, and describe how Fox finally gave the go-ahead for production to begin in 2007. Comments from the late visual effects pioneer Stan Winston are also included.

A major thread is the development of the groundbreaking performance capture techniques that allowed actors to drive every movement of the digital Na'vi characters on screen, and the film follows how these methods advanced over the course of production. It includes footage of the 2006 auditions and screen tests of Sam Worthington, Zoe Saldaña and Joel Moore, and a moment in which Cameron explains to Sigourney Weaver that her character's surname will have to change from Shipley to Augustine so that audiences do not confuse her with Ripley, her role in Aliens.

Interviewees include Cameron, Landau, Worthington, Saldaña, Weaver, Stephen Lang, Giovanni Ribisi and Michelle Rodriguez, alongside casting director Margery Simkin and many of the artists and crew members who worked on the film. Reviewers of the collector's edition singled the documentary out among its extras; Slant Magazine described it as a groovy survey of the film's evolution and the filmmaker's journey, and Hollywood in Hi-Def highlighted its archival material on the early performance capture experiments and casting.

Since her last adventure, the butterfly fairy Mariposa has become royal historian of Flutterfield. On the recommendation of Prince Carlos, Queen Marabella appoints her ambassador to the Crystal Fairies of Shimmervale. Centuries earlier, Shimmervale's king accused the butterfly fairies of stealing Crystallite, the source of light and warmth for his realm, and the two peoples have lived as enemies ever since, each spreading rumors about the other. Doubting herself, Mariposa receives from Carlos a glowing flower holding Flutterfield's most precious magic and sets off with her furry companion Zee.

In Shimmervale, the suspicious King Regellius gives her a cold welcome, but she quickly befriends his shy daughter, Princess Catania, and learns that outsiders are forbidden to touch Crystallite, above all the powerful Heart Crystal. Catania confides that eight years earlier the dark fairy Gillion, refused a piece of Crystallite by her father, tried to kidnap her; her wings were broken in the attack, and although they healed she has not flown since. Mariposa also realizes that the king only invited her because he believes butterfly fairies are warriors who could teach his army. As a token of friendship, Catania gives Mariposa her Crystallite pendant, and Mariposa gives her the glowing flower.

At the Crystal Ball, guests spot the pendant and accuse Mariposa of theft, and the king banishes her despite Catania's defense. Gillion then attacks, turning the kingdom's crystals and people to stone. Encouraged by Mariposa, Catania overcomes her fear of flying, and together they restore the Heart Crystal, which rewards both with new wings. Catania chooses to forgive Gillion and offers her Crystallite, restoring her youth, and the king, admitting he misjudged Mariposa, makes peace with Flutterfield.

The film was released on DVD in the United States on 27 August 2013.

At its core, Antboy is a coming-of-age story about a shy and awkward teenager named Pelle who finds his place in the world when he develops extraordinary abilities. As Pelle navigates his new powers, he must confront his own insecurities and learn to accept himself for who he is. The film suggests that true strength lies not in physical prowess, but in embracing one's uniqueness and finding confidence within oneself.

The movie also touches on the theme of social isolation and the importance of human connection. Pelle's struggles to fit in at school and his difficulties forming relationships with his peers serve as a catalyst for his transformation into Antboy. Through his superhero alter ego, Pelle is able to connect with others and find a sense of belonging, highlighting the value of empathy and understanding.

Furthermore, Antboy pokes fun at traditional superhero tropes, using humor to subvert expectations and challenge societal norms. The film's lighthearted tone and comedic approach make it an entertaining ride, while also offering a commentary on the pressures of conformity and the importance of individuality.

Overall, Antboy is a heartwarming and humorous tale that celebrates self-acceptance, friendship, and the power of embracing one's true nature.

A prologue recounts the legend of Numbuh 0, a boy who long ago discovered the Book of KND and its 2x4 technology and led a revolt against Grandfather, a tyrant who forced children to make tapioca in his factories, stripping him of his power. In the present, Numbuh 1, leader of Sector V, still believes the legend. While the Kids Next Door fight off simultaneous villain attacks on their museum and Moonbase, Father steals the Recommissioning Module, a device that restores lost memories, and uses it to revive Grandfather, who promptly takes over the coalition of villains. Grandfather begins turning children, and anyone who was once a child, into wrinkled, tapioca-making "Senior Citizombies", overrunning the organization and converting treehouses around the world into tapioca factories.

Blaming himself, Numbuh 1 becomes one of the last free operatives and sets out to find and recommission Numbuh 0, only to discover that the legendary hero is his own father, Monty Uno. Further revelations follow: Father is Monty's brother, making him Numbuh 1's uncle and Grandfather his grandfather, and the Delightful Children from Down the Lane are the lost Sector Z, brainwashed long ago. While Monty holds off Grandfather, who is searching for the Book of KND, Numbuh 1 and his restored teammates bring the Moonbase crashing down on the villain, and Monty lures him into a decommissioning chamber, erasing both their memories and restoring the world. Afterwards Numbuh 1, now keeper of the book, writes in it, "We are Kids Next Door."

Operation Z.E.R.O. premiered on Cartoon Network on August 11, 2006. Warburton said the script took about two months to write, compared with the usual two weeks for an episode.

A prologue set a thousand years earlier shows the genie Gigi Grant breaking the rules of her lantern to stop her shadow sister, Whisp, from using an eclipse to seize power through the last wish of a finder. In the present, a new school year begins at Monster High, and Clawdeen Wolf's little sister Howleen, tired of being overlooked, is determined to become popular. Serving detention in the school attic with Frankie Stein, Clawdeen, Draculaura, Lagoona Blue and Ghoulia Yelps, she discovers the lantern and frees Gigi, who grants her not three but thirteen wishes, unwittingly releasing Whisp as well.

Howleen first uses her wishes to help her friends, getting the ghouls out of detention, making Abbey Bominable student body president and putting Clawd and his friends on a dangerous television show. Under Whisp's secret influence, however, she wishes herself popular, turns Cleo de Nile into a nobody and banishes Clawdeen into the lantern, leaving a shadow double behind. Each wish has a dark side, and the school turns upside down. Gigi, forbidden to influence her finder, confides in Frankie, revealing that Whisp plans to use the coming eclipse to replace everyone with shadow versions and rule the world. Frankie, Draculaura and Ghoulia have Howleen wish them into the lantern, where they rescue Clawdeen and search for the shards of a shattered magic mirror. Returning on magic carpets in time for the eclipse, they join Howleen's shy shadow friend Twyla, who assembles the mirror and breaks Whisp's spell. Howleen undoes her earlier wishes and spends the last one freeing Gigi while letting Whisp become a real genie of the lantern.

The voice cast includes America Young as Howleen, Jonquil Goode as Gigi, Whisp and Twyla, Salli Saffioti as Clawdeen and Cleo, Kate Higgins as Frankie, Debi Derryberry as Draculaura and Erin Fitzgerald as Abbey. The film was also released in several European countries that October.

The story is a simple, almost wordless comic episode. When an ice cream truck rolls through the neighbourhood, Margo, Edith and little Agnes race after it on their bicycles. Agnes, the youngest, still struggles on her bike and falls behind, then takes a tumble while pedalling, leaving her disappointed and in tears. A trio of Minions, moved by her distress, decides to help her catch up. Applying their usual eccentric ingenuity, they put her through a training regimen, with one Minion acting as her coach, and build her a gleaming unicorn-themed motorcycle.

Riding her new machine, Agnes finally reaches her sisters, but just as she is about to get her ice cream, a jewel thief hijacks the ice cream van and speeds off. Furious at losing her treat, Agnes chases the van through town, shouting for her ice cream, and inadvertently causes the thief to crash, which makes her a local hero. Her motorcycle is wrecked in the process, but in the end she manages to ride her old bicycle without stabilisers and declares that she likes it better anyway, not least because the Minions have secretly fitted it with a button that transforms it into a robotic suit.

The short reunites much of the feature's voice cast. Miranda Cosgrove voices Margo, Dana Gaier voices Edith and Elsie Fisher voices Agnes, while Pierre Coffin provides the voices of the Minions. Dave Rosenbaum voices the ice cream vendor, co-director Régis Schuller voices the jewel thief, and Steve Carell appears uncredited as Gru. Like the other bonus shorts made for the franchise's home video releases, it extends the slapstick, dialogue-light humour of the Minions into a self-contained story built around a single gag-driven situation.

In Shipwreck City, Scarlett and Giselle are preparing for their weddings in front of the same mirror when they realize they are about to marry the same man: both wear identical rings from Captain Jack Sparrow. A curtain then rises to reveal a room full of eager pirates and a banner announcing an auction of wenches as brides. The two women, who believe the money is being raised for them, compete for attention as the bids climb, then brawl on stage, which only drives the price higher, until the Marquis D'Avis buys them both for 700 pieces of silver and two goats. When the Auctioneer shackles them and declares that the proceeds are his, since Jack traded them to him fair and square under the Pirate Code, the crowd turns ugly. The stern guardian of the Code, Mungard, threatens anyone who disrespects it, but Giselle slaps him, a stray pistol shot sets off chaos, and Mungard, hearing Jack's name, fires and hits the Code book itself. He orders the shocked pirates to keep silent on pain of losing their tongues, and Cotton promptly assures him that "mum's the word". Escaping by boat, the brides vow to slap Jack when they next see him, and Scarlett reveals that she pulled four nails from his boat, explaining why it is sinking when he first appears in The Curse of the Black Pearl.

Byrkit, a conceptual consultant on the trilogy, shot the short in late 2006 in three days on the Shipwreck Cove sets left over from At World's End before they were demolished. It was released on 18 October 2011 as an exclusive in the Pirates of the Caribbean Four-Movie Collection Blu-ray set. Reviewing it, Chronique Disney called it funny, respectful and well paced, faithful to the spirit of the first three films.

Duff plays Isabella "Belle" Everhart, who leaves her California hometown and heads north on an assignment from her father, Rex (Howell). She is to catalogue the contents of the grand Lowell estate, a mansion set amid vineyards, which its owner, Hunter Lowell (Gonzalez), wants sold before Christmas. Hunter is gruff, preoccupied and openly cold toward her, and only accepts her presence because he is in a hurry to get the job done.

Belle loves the work, especially the mansion's library of rare books, and befriends the housekeeper, Angie (Wilson). Her eagerness to prepare the house for the sale gets her into trouble when she rearranges a room she was told to leave alone, but the incident breaks the ice, and Hunter tries to make amends for his behaviour. As they spend more time together, his icy manner begins to melt and the two grow close. Their budding romance is thrown into confusion when Belle's long-time suitor, Tony (Famiglietti), arrives in town with her father, determined to win her with grand gestures and a few lies that send mixed signals to Hunter and add chaos to the holiday season.

The film drew modest notices typical of the made-for-television Christmas romance. The blog Tranquil Dreams found the story predictable and somewhat disjointed, lacking depth, but praised the chemistry and charm of Duff and Gonzalez and admired the picturesque estate, with its barn and covered bridge, and the homey small-town setting. The same review criticised the heavy-handed direction, including repeated, overly dramatic scenes of a shirtless Hunter's morning runs and an orchestral score that at one point drowned out the dialogue, concluding that the film was average but fairly enjoyable. HallmarkDB described it as largely standard for the genre, lifted slightly by its enemies-to-lovers arc.

Lyosha is a talented young advertising creative who has come to conquer Moscow, but nothing is going his way. He has no work, no money for rent and no personal life, his parents nag him, and a project he spent a year on has found no takers. At a casting session at an advertising agency, he makes a poor impression, arriving badly dressed, unsure of himself and carrying a broken laptop. Then things get worse: he is fined for parking, evicted from his flat and left to haul his sofa to a park with a friend, where he dreams of being able to solve every problem with the press of a single button. Luck comes from an unexpected direction when he meets a mysterious figure, Snoop Dogg himself, who gives him a magic laptop. Whatever Lyosha writes as a status on his social network page immediately comes true. He gains money, an expensive car, new clothes, a house and travel, and even becomes the boss of the agency that refused to hire him. The one thing the computer cannot give him is real love, which he must find without search queries, and he learns that everything in life has its price.

The film was released in Russia on 12 December 2013. Russian critics treated it as a light diversion. Yevgeny Ukhov of Film.ru called it a frivolous, disposable comedy with a very obvious, rather adolescent moral that could amuse undemanding viewers, finding the scenes in which Lyosha discovers the laptop's powers the funniest but the selfish hero hard to sympathize with, and singling out Bondarchuk's caricatured character as the liveliest presence. Kinoafisha's editor compared the story to Pushkin's fairy tale of the fisherman and the fish for today's youth, while Kino Mail.ru noted parallels with Bruce Almighty.

Kelly Sheridan voices Lumina, a cheerful seventeen-year-old mermaid who can make pearls glow and move at her command. She lives on a remote reef with her seahorse friend Kuda (Katie Crown) and her stern aunt Scylla (Trish Pattendon), who forbids her to show her power. In the royal capital, King Nereus and Queen Lorelei still mourn a daughter lost years earlier, and the king's brother-in-law Caligo (John Novak) arranges a royal ball at which his son Fergis, heir in the absence of the princess, is to find a wife. Caligo secretly sends his eel henchman Murray to force Scylla, a potion-maker, to poison the king at the ball.

Finding the invitation Scylla left behind, Lumina sets off for the city with Kuda, befriending a lonely spiny fish named Spike along the way. There she becomes a celebrated hairstylist at the salon of the octopus Madame Ruckus, using her pearls to create dazzling styles, meets the visiting Prince Delphin, and watches the gentle Fergis, who would rather be a botanist, fall for her co-worker Cora. Caligo, meanwhile, realises from a hidden royal bracelet that Lumina is the missing princess and has her imprisoned, but she escapes using her powers.

At the ball Lumina knocks the poisoned cup from the king's hand. When Scylla tries to reveal the plot, Caligo pushes her onto one of Spike's venomous spines, and she confesses that she took Lumina away as a baby on Caligo's orders but chose to raise her instead of harming her. Fergis supplies a rare lily that cures her, and Lumina uses her pearls to stop Caligo. The queen reveals that she shares the same pearl magic, a royal gift, confirming Lumina's identity; the princess is reunited with her parents and asks that Scylla and Kuda join her at the palace.

The voice cast also includes Mark Oliver as Nereus, Rebecca Shoichet as Lorelei, Simon Hill as Fergis, Peter New as Murray and Kathleen Barr as Madame Ruckus.

The story revolves around a centuries-old legend about a missing vampire queen and a long-lost stone known as the Vampire's Heart. The vampire community has had no queen for 400 years, ever since the last heir, Elissabat, ran away on the day of her coronation, and the legend has inspired a popular, melodramatic movie franchise, Vampire Majesty, in which two suitors compete for the queen. Draculaura, whose family once belonged to the vampire court, dislikes how the films depict vampire royalty. When the vampire council demands that the interim ruler, the greedy Lord Stoker, produce the missing heir within a week, he convinces Draculaura that she is the rightful heir in order to manipulate her, and even tries to force her to marry him. She and her best friends are whisked off to Transylvania for the coronation, but they soon discover that the search for the true queen is not over. Hunting for the Vampire's Heart, Draculaura, Cleo de Nile, Robecca and Hoodude Voodoo follow clues to New Goreleans, Londoom and Barcelgroana, picking up new friends along the way: the aspiring cinematographer Honey Swamp, the screenwriting student Clawdia Wolf and the makeup artist Viperine Gorgon. The trail ends in the film capital Hauntlywood, where the famous actress Veronica Von Vamp is rumored to know where Elissabat is. Back at school, the students hold a "cute court" to decide which vampire actor is more attractive.

Universal Pictures Home Entertainment released the film on DVD and Blu-ray on 25 March 2014, with three 2D animated shorts as extras. Reviews were moderate. High Def Digest found it less catchy than the previous entry, with a slow middle section, but enjoyed its jabs at pop culture and the Twilight craze and its strong, funny finale in Hauntlywood, recommending it mainly to fans. Common Sense Media found the plot amusing in spoofing fan debates over fictional love triangles, but rated it for ages eight and up because of its focus on teen crushes.

Liotti plays Alex, a handsome and successful 37-year-old advertising executive who, after years of hesitation, decides to settle down and proposes to his girlfriend Elena (Irene Montalà), only to be turned down. Shaken, he is distracted at the wheel and lightly knocks over Niki (Bloyd), a spirited 17-year-old in her final year of secondary school, who is riding a scooter. Niki charms him with her cheek and vitality, has him drive her wherever she likes, and soon persuades him into something he had never imagined: a romance with a woman twenty years his junior. The story is framed by the narration of a secretive detective.

The relationship brings the couple joy and plenty of trouble. Alex's colleagues at the agency insist on meeting Niki's friends, leading to a group date with mixed results; Niki, after her friends suggest that Alex might be secretly married, follows him and smashes his car window in a jealous rage on seeing him with a woman who turns out to be his sister. After a schoolmate of Niki's mocks Alex as a "grandpa" and punches him at a nightclub, he begins to doubt whether the age gap can be bridged. A romantic trip to Paris for Niki's eighteenth birthday briefly restores their hopes, but back home Alex ends the affair, saying they come from different worlds, and Niki calls him a coward. Weeks later he realises he cannot live without her, and the two are reunited on a holiday island.

The supporting cast includes Andrea Duro, Cristina Brondo, Jan Cornet and Pablo Chiapella. Critics were largely unimpressed. Pere Vall of Fotogramas awarded it two stars out of five, singling out Bloyd, her friends, Chiapella, the cinematography and the Barcelona setting amid many laughable scenes, while Jonathan Holland of The Hollywood Reporter called it a slick, superficial forbidden-love fantasy whose calculated lack of irony gave it a certain appeal.

With Christmas approaching, the little monkey George and his friend Ted, the Man with the Yellow Hat, count down the days, decorate and look for ways to make the time fly, but each secretly faces the same problem: neither knows what to give the other. George draws a Christmas list full of seemingly random shapes that Ted cannot decipher, nor can the doorman or Chef Pisghetti when Ted shows it to them, so Ted asks George to surprise him instead. George decides to make his friend a present but cannot settle on what. Meanwhile, Betsy struggles to write a new carol for her Aunt Margaret, since every Christmas subject seems to have its song already.

The preparations bring a series of gentle mishaps. A trip to the country to buy a tree ends with George climbing to the top of one and toppling a whole row; a snowplough built by Professor Wiseman, which George hopes will be the perfect gift, goes awry; and a small fire brings a fire engine. At Betsy's Christmas Eve performance, her new song turns out to be about George himself. In a dream inspired by Dickens's A Christmas Carol, the clockmaker shows Ted imagined lives in which other friends give George a perfect existence, and he realises that his friend wanted the toys in a shop window. On Christmas morning, George presents Ted with a roll of wrapping paper illustrated with the story of their Christmas.

Frank Welker voices George and Jeff Bennett the Man with the Yellow Hat, with Rino Romano narrating and Grey DeLisle, Jim Cummings, E. G. Daily, Rob Paulsen and Rolonda Watts among the supporting cast. Animated Views found the special slight but highly pleasing, praising its old-fashioned, storybook animation and amusing dialogue, while Common Sense Media judged it suitable for children aged three and up.

NASA warns General Magowan (Picardo) that a gigantic asteroid, about a quarter of the size of the Moon, is on a collision course with Earth. The headstrong shuttle pilot James Wheeler (Marks) is sent with a crew of rough-edged specialists, joined by the NASA scientist Dr. Gordon (Hu), to plant nuclear weapons that will push it off course. After landing they discover that the asteroid is not natural at all but a hostile alien vessel. Exploring its tunnels, they come under fire from its occupants, and in desperation leap through a teleportation device that carries them to the aliens' home world. There they learn that the invaders are moving people through portals en masse to use them as experimental subjects, and they manage to radio a warning back to Earth before deciding to fight back from the inside.

Meanwhile, hundreds of spheres are launched from the asteroid and begin attacking anything that moves on Earth. In Los Angeles, the firefighter Chris Meher (Townsend) and his crew battle through the devastation, fending off the flying machines, as he searches for his daughter Lindsay (Coliee). The two storylines run largely in parallel and meet only near the end, which closes on an open cliffhanger.

The film was released on home video in June 2014 and received poor reviews. Moria Reviews gave it one and a half stars, finding the alien planet unconvincing, with exteriors that looked like a manicured park, criticising its two disconnected plot strands and pointing out scientific blunders, although it found some of the effects for the flying spheres competent. Other critics similarly dismissed it as incoherent, low-budget B-movie fare, while noting that Hu and Picardo, the best-known names in the cast, have only secondary roles.

The story follows Niki Jumonji (played by Showtimes), an American who has been infected with a deadly virus that turns people into zombies after they are bitten. Niki, along with his friend and colleague, Takashi (played by Hiroki Hasegawa), is sent to Japan to investigate the outbreak of the virus.

Upon arrival in Tokyo, Niki discovers that the city is rapidly descending into chaos as the infected begin to multiply at an alarming rate. The government has sealed off the city, but it's clear that they are not equipped to handle the situation.

As Niki navigates the deserted streets, he encounters various survivors, including a young woman named Yumi (played by Kanna Hashimoto) who becomes his ally in the fight against the infected. Together, they try to find a way to escape the city and prevent the virus from spreading further.

However, as the days pass, Niki begins to experience strange visions and hallucinations, hinting that he may be developing symptoms of the virus himself. The line between reality and fantasy becomes increasingly blurred, leaving Niki questioning his own sanity.

As the situation spirals out of control, Niki and Yumi discover a mysterious underground bunker where they hope to find a cure for the virus. However, upon arrival, they are met with a shocking revelation: the true source of the outbreak is not what they expected.

The movie's climax features an intense confrontation between Niki and the mastermind behind the outbreak, who reveals a sinister plot to use the virus as a means of population control. In the end, Niki must make a difficult choice that will determine the fate of humanity.

Throughout the film, Sato explores themes of isolation, paranoia, and the breakdown of society in the face of catastrophic events. The movie's atmosphere is tense and foreboding, with a sense of impending doom that permeates every scene.

Overall, I Am a Hero is a gripping and unsettling thriller that will keep viewers on the edge of their seats until the very end. With its unique blend of science fiction and horror elements, it has become a cult classic among fans of the genre.

The series it chronicles aired on Nickelodeon for three seasons from 2005 to 2008 and follows Aang, a twelve-year-old boy who is the last of the Air Nomads and the Avatar, the only person able to bend all four elements. The documentary traces this world back to a single sketch by Konietzko showing a bald boy, a tall animal with an arrow on its head and a robot monkey with a futuristic staff. The arrow migrated to the boy's head, and the creatures evolved into the characters Appa and Momo. At about the same time, DiMartino had become fascinated by Ernest Shackleton's struggle to survive in the Antarctic, and combining that polar setting with the idea of "fire people" attacking "water people" led to the concept of four nations.

The film describes the pitch to Nickelodeon development executive Eric Coleman, the demanding production of the pilot, for which Konietzko spent several months in South Korea and designs had to be simplified, and the order of thirteen episodes that followed its success with young test audiences. It then turns to the wider crew. Martial arts instructors Sifu Kisu and Manuel Rodríguez explain how real fighting styles, filmed in sparring sessions, provided the basis for the animated bending; director Giancarlo Volpe recalls the cinematic camera angles the creators demanded; Jeremy Zuckerman and Benjamin Wynn of the Track Team describe the unusual instruments behind the show's music and sound; and voice director Andrea Romano explains how she guided the actors' performances.

The documentary closes with the making of the finale, which the creators always intended as the definitive end of the story. To make it their best work, the Track Team recorded a live string orchestra for the first time, and the crew, with friends and family, gathered at the Paramount theater to watch the ending on a big screen.

Grace, an eighteen-year-old raised in a small town, has lived a sheltered life under the suspicious eye of her devout and domineering grandmother. Helen never recovered from the fall of Grace's mother, who left the Church, became pregnant and died giving birth to her daughter, so Grace has grown up with a Bible in her hand. Going away to college is her first chance to see more of the world. She is unsure about her outgoing roommate Jessica but drawn to Brad, a handsome classmate. However, she has started seeing strange visions and feeling unwell, with symptoms resembling the psychosis her mother seemed to suffer before her death. After a party where she has a few drinks with Brad and Jessica, an episode lands her in hospital, and Helen takes her home, forcing her back into a strict Catholic routine. There Grace uncovers secrets about her mother's death while her grandmother becomes convinced that the Devil is trying to claim her. As the entity inside her grows stronger and acts through her body, the stoic Father John attempts an exorcism, leading to a violent finale.

The film was released on DVD in the United States on 28 October 2014. Reviewers generally found the story thin and derivative of The Exorcist but credited the first-person approach. DVD Talk praised how Chan conveyed Fast's performance though she is rarely seen, and Shaye's turn as the repressed grandmother, but felt the director did not push his style far enough, calling the film a rental. Flickering Myth considered it a brave attempt to refresh a limited subgenre, admiring Shaye and Dale while criticizing the cheap computer effects and the demonic voice, and found that the film gains energy once Grace returns home.

As Monster High celebrates its 200th anniversary, Frankie Stein and her friends Draculaura, Clawdeen, Lagoona, Cleo and Ghoulia agree to help drama teacher Mr. Where stage a play about the school's history. Frankie fails a class project on her family heritage because her parents will not talk about her grandfather, Victor Frankenstein. Robecca Steam, whose mad scientist father, the former teacher Hexiciah Steam, vanished long ago, leads the ghouls, along with Venus, Jinafire and a meddling Toralei, to his workshop in the catacombs to find his journal. When Toralei pulls a lever, a machine sends them all back 200 years to 1814.

In the past, Frankie meets Sparky, a student obsessed with creating life, and tells him that her grandfather achieved it. Sparky secretly follows the girls through the time portal, which malfunctions: Frankie and Ghoulia return intact, but their friends arrive fused into four hybrid monsters, Dracubecca, Cleolei, Clawvenus and Lagoonafire, who struggle to control their new bodies and powers during rehearsals. A group of newcomers, the Hybrids, among them Neighthan Rot, who had seemed unfriendly, help the fused ghouls adapt. Meanwhile, Sparky steals a part of the time machine and builds Creature 4.0, which goes on a rampage, wrecks the play and captures Frankie's friends one by one. Frankie spends all her spark to save and separate them, and Sparky realises that emotion is what gives her true life. Dying, she learns that Sparky is in fact her grandfather. With Hexiciah's help, the whole school shares its sparks to revive her, the two men return to their own time, and the play resumes with a message that every monster, flaws and all, is welcome at Monster High.

The voice cast includes Kate Higgins as Frankie, Debi Derryberry as Draculaura, Salli Saffioti as Clawdeen and Cleo, Laura Bailey as Lagoona and Headmistress Bloodgood, America Young as Toralei, Haviland Stillwell as Avea, Geeg Friedman as Bonita, and Dave B. Mitchell as Hexiciah Steam.

Billionaire William Hadden has gathered twelve of the legendary crystal skulls, artifacts he claims are more than five thousand years old, at his headquarters in Vienna. When his associate Mitchell delivers what is believed to be the thirteenth, it turns out to be a fake, and uniting it with the others unleashes a massive electromagnetic pulse that kills two lab workers, cripples much of Europe and creates a second magnetic field that wreaks havoc on the world's weather. In Sweden, John Winston and his brother Terry are exploring ruins their father visited before his supposed death; a booby trap brings down the cave, and Terry is killed. Back in the United States, John finds his classes cancelled, and Sienna, Hadden's daughter, recruits him to find the thirteenth skull. Hadden reveals he brought the skulls together hoping they could cure his cancer and that the growing vortex will tear the Earth apart within about a day, while Colonel Bailey prepares a nuclear strike on Vienna. Pursued by a secret brotherhood determined to stop them, John, Sienna and Mitchell decipher his father's notes and trace the skull to the Visočica hill in Bosnia, where they find John's father alive among the skull's guardians. He turns on the cult and helps them escape with the skull, but is fatally shot. John places it with the others just in time, the storm vanishes, and Hadden, who dies, is entombed with the skulls.

The film was poorly received. Richard Scheib of Moria gave it one star, describing it as a cheap disaster movie crossed with Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull that delivers on neither, with its catastrophe conveyed mostly by newscasters and the skulls' origin never explained, though he found Burgi a serviceable hero. HorrorNews.net criticized its acting, effects, plot holes and pseudo-science.

The film opens with two police officers entering a house where a family has been murdered; inside, they are attacked and killed by the family's knife-wielding son, Zachary. Five years later, newly separated from her husband Jonathan (Muldoon), Alyson Simon (Pressly) moves into the large old house in the countryside with her nine-year-old daughter Claire (Rogers). The estate agent has kept the killings secret, and Alyson only learns of them after the move. Exploring the house, Claire finds a doll left behind by the previous occupants and soon develops a dangerous obsession with it.

Claire's behaviour grows increasingly disturbing, and deaths begin to pile up, starting with the apparent suicide of Jonathan's new girlfriend during one of Claire's visits. Alyson visits Zachary in a psychiatric institution in search of answers, learning nothing before he later escapes. Every attempt to get rid of the doll fails, as it keeps returning to Claire, and a voodoo-like bond forms between them, so that whatever happens to one happens to the other. Claire's therapist, Dr. Freeman (Bell), mistakes the injuries she suffers when her parents try to destroy the toy for signs of abuse, but is killed after realising she lied. Alyson's friend Elena Carranza (Justina Machado), a professor who studies the paranormal, takes the doll to her laboratory and suggests that removing its eyes will break the connection, but she too falls victim to the possessed girl. In a final struggle at the house, Jonathan gouges out the doll's eyes and breaks the curse, and the reconciled parents decide to sell the house and give their marriage another chance.

The cast also includes Marina Sirtis, Mark DeCarlo and Joey Luthman as the adult Zachary. German-language reviews found the film lacking in suspense and derivative of Sinister and Child's Play, praising the performances of Rogers and Bell but less impressed by Pressly and the dialogue.

The story unfolds among cornfields. Young Kyle brings his older brother, Jason, out to the cornfields to show him something strange that has been happening for a week: whenever he throws a basketball into the corn, it is thrown back. Jason is astonished when the ball returns, and even more so by what steps out of the field, a deadly alien creature built like a sleek war machine, which the filmmakers call Aeon. The two brothers soon find themselves entangled in a top-secret government operation as the military moves in, and the creature, despite its menace, shows mercy toward innocent life and protects its young human playmates when the soldiers launch an all-out assault.

Weinstein described the short as a love letter to the action-adventure and science fiction films of the 1980s and 1990s. The production was completed in under a year of part-time work on a post-production budget of only a few thousand dollars, which meant building a live-action CGI pipeline and render farm to create computer-generated Apache helicopters, birds, corn, the basketball and the alien itself. The film became a viral success, drawing more than ten million combined views and appearing on major short film websites.

Critics agreed that its effects were its main attraction. Short of the Week saw the influence of Steven Spielberg, J. J. Abrams's Super 8 and Iron Man, noting the coming-of-age thread but saying it would win no prizes for originality while catching the eye of talent scouts. Singularity Hub praised the alien's design but found the story recycled and the military response clichéd. Cinema Crazed was more enthusiastic, calling it The Iron Giant meets Predator and arguing that it deserved a big-budget feature treatment.

Kara is a modern princess of the kingdom of Windermere with a fairly ordinary life and ambitious goals, such as starting a community garden, who would rather fly aircraft than attend formal balls. Her loving parents, however, are so overprotective that they refuse to let her take any risks, which is especially frustrating because her best friends Madison and Makalya are scientific prodigies whose inventions constantly tempt her toward adventure. Unknown to the royal family, Baron von Ravendale, one of the king's trusted advisers, is brewing a potion as part of a scheme to destroy the king and seize the throne for himself.

When the potion escapes his control, a butterfly that swallows it becomes a magical creature, and its kiss gives Kara superpowers, including strength, agility and the ability to fly. With her friends' help she becomes the superheroine Super Sparkle, secretly rescuing citizens from fires, collapsing construction sites and robbers. Her jealous cousin Corinne discovers her secret, captures the butterfly and uses its power to transform herself into Dark Sparkle, and the two compete to be the town's top hero. When the Baron drinks a potion that grants him magical powers and unleashes lava from a volcano on the castle and the town, the rivals must set aside their competition and fight him together to save their families and the kingdom.

Released on DVD and digital platforms by Universal in early 2015, the film added a superhero dimension to the Barbie brand and introduced a new line of dolls. Common Sense Media found it a fun adventure with more action and peril than earlier Barbie films, praising the heroine's resourcefulness and her scientifically gifted friends, while the Australian Council on Children and the Media highlighted its message that working together is better than being alone.

Derbez plays María Laura Medina, nicknamed "Mala", a talented but luckless actress who, disillusioned with men and unable to find acting work, earns a living by putting her skills to a different use. Hired by women who suspect their boyfriends, she adopts a series of disguises, accents and personas to seduce the men and expose whether they are unfaithful, concluding from experience that virtually all men are weak. Her big break finally seems to arrive when an important producer offers her the lead in a television series, but on one condition: Mala must make the producer's ex-boyfriend fall in love with her and then make him pay for all the suffering he caused.

The target is Santiago (Ochmann), a wealthy businessman whom Mala cannot stand at first and who appears to be an arrogant boor with no interest in the arts. As she works her way into his life, Santiago breaks the pattern she has come to expect, revealing a hidden side as a musician and philanthropist and opening up to her about his past. Mala's professional convictions are shaken as she realises she is falling for him, and she must decide whether to complete the job that could launch her career. Her friends Kika (Aurora Papile) and Pablo (Luis Arrieta) provide comic support, while Daniela Schmidt plays the scheming Patricia; the cast also features Juan Diego Covarrubias, José Ron and Iván Sánchez, with a cameo by Eugenio Derbez.

At Monster High, the school for the children of famous monsters in the town of New Salem, the ghostly student blogger Spectra Vondergeist is desperate for a juicy story, while Draculaura becomes convinced she is being haunted. Spectra reveals a secret she has never shared: close by lies a hidden spirit world with its own all-ghost school, Haunted High, which she once attended. Hoping to find help and perhaps a scoop, since there has not been a haunting in ages, not since the legend of the Red Lady, she heads there and fails to return. Led by Clawdeen Wolf, Draculaura, Rochelle Goyle, Twyla and Sirena Von Boo set out after her, entering a realm where non-ghost monsters are feared as "solids." Twyla, daughter of the Boogie Man, devises a way to disguise the friends as ghosts so they can slip into the school. There they find a student body crushed by the strict Principal Revenant, who rules with the help of her Hall Moanitors and punishes pupils with detention chains that would keep Spectra trapped forever. Befriended by Haunted High students such as River Styxx, Vandala Doubloons, the painter Portergeist and Kiyomi Haunterly, the ghouls work to expose Revenant's scheme and her hateful rumors, unravel the mystery of the Red Lady and free their friend.

The film was released on home video in the United States on 24 March 2015. Common Sense Media's Renee Longstreet called it an engaging, mildly suspenseful story that stands on its own beyond selling toys, praising its humor, bright style and message about the harm of gossip and rumors while noting the familiar skimpy costumes. A DVD Talk family review described it as fun and not scary, recommending it for children aged seven to ten.

The film follows Ronaldo from his humble childhood on the island of Madeira to his status as a global sports star and celebrity. It portrays a poor upbringing and a solitary boy whose constant companion was a football. In one of the comparatively rare passages in which he speaks directly to the camera, Ronaldo explains that there was no single reason he took up the game, citing his father and brother as influences rather than claiming a lifelong dream. He joined the local club Andorinha at eight and moved to Sporting Lisbon at twelve, after scouts noticed his talent.

The documentary recounts the turning point of August 2003, when, after Sporting played Manchester United, the English club's players urged manager Sir Alex Ferguson to sign the teenager. Ferguson, presented as a father figure, gave him the famous number 7 shirt, and Ronaldo went on to become a superstar in England, regarded as a hero by some and an arrogant villain by others, before his move to Real Madrid. Combining interviews, archival and recent match footage and dramatised re-enactments, the film charts his awards, his rivalry and constant comparison with Lionel Messi, and his gradual maturing from self-absorbed playboy into a philanthropist and role model. Among the commentators is West Ham United's youth development director Anthony Carr, who explains what scouts look for in young players.

Reviews were mixed. Tom Keogh of Video Librarian gave it three out of five, calling it a brisk and exciting profile and recommending it. Charles Low of Kettle Mag found Cumberbatch's narration tasteful if puzzling and appreciated some insightful interviews, but felt the film zig-zagged between key moments, padded itself with general football commentary and pointless contributors such as an astrologer and skateboarder Tony Hawk, and relied on odd re-enactments that left it somewhere between a celebrity documentary and a sports broadcast, offering less insight into the man himself than he had hoped.

After a hectic kite chase in the park, George and Ted are approached by Houston, an official of a space agency, who offers George a once-in-a-lifetime mission. As part of a project to stop the floods devastating a region of Central Africa, George is to fly into orbit, retrieve a device called the Regional Dam Synchronizer from a broken satellite, and bring it back so that it can be installed on a dam, where its antenna will coordinate the other dams in the area. Ted is reluctant at first, but agrees after George's pleading, on the condition that he complete the astronaut training, which he does.

The first part of the mission goes smoothly, and George retrieves the device, but during the return his curiosity sends the capsule's systems haywire and it plunges toward Earth. George ejects and lands somewhere in the African jungle, while the capsule disappears with the device still on board. Houston, his assistant Andrew and Ted travel to Africa, where search teams scour an area hundreds of miles wide; eventually Ted sets out on his own, cut off from contact with Houston. Back in the land of his birth, George meets Dr. Kulinda, a veterinarian who runs an animal preserve. The friends must find each other, recover the device and install it before a huge storm bearing down on the region can ravage the jungle, and in the end they complete the mission in time.

The film was released on DVD by Universal Pictures Home Entertainment on 23 June 2015 and later aired on PBS Kids. It was the last film in the series to use traditional animation. Reviewers praised its fast, suspenseful yet gentle storytelling, bright visuals and lack of a conventional villain, with the storm serving as the main threat, as well as songs such as "Ordinary Superman".

The story continues from the first film, in which Eren and his friends Mikasa and Armin joined the Survey Corps to fight the man-eating giants called Titans after their town was destroyed. A flashback shows the young Eren being forcibly injected with an experimental serum by his father before military police seize his parents and burn their home. In the present, Eren, who can now transform into a Titan, is captured by the commander Kubal, who regards him as a threat to humanity; Mikasa does nothing to defend him, and his ally Souda is killed. Before Eren can be executed, a Titan bursts in and carries him off.

Eren wakes in a mysterious bunker with Shikishima, who reveals that the Titans originated in a failed military experiment and plans a coup against a corrupt government that uses the walls and fear of the giants to oppress its people. Meanwhile Hans, Mikasa and the others recover an unexploded bomb from Eren's home town, hoping to seal the breach in the outer wall. When Shikishima reveals that he intends to blow up the capital instead and let the Titans liberate humanity, Eren turns against him, transforms and defeats him. In the final battle Kubal turns into the Colossal Titan, Jean is killed, and Shikishima sacrifices himself by placing the bomb in the giant's mouth; the blast seals the wall, and Eren and Mikasa stand on top of it looking out at the ocean.

Barbie stars as Princess Courtney, a modern royal heading to an island summer camp for the first time. On the island are two rival camps: Camp Royalty, for young princes and princesses, and Camp Pop, for aspiring musicians. A registration mix-up swaps Courtney's name with that of Erika Juno (Chiara Zanni), a famous rock star who has cancelled her tour hoping to make real friends at Camp Pop, so the princess lands among the musicians and the singer among the royals. The camp heads, the stern Lady Anne (Nicole Oliver) of Camp Royalty and Finn Oxford (Michael Dobson) of Camp Pop, share an old rivalry. When Lady Anne hears Erika sing, she fakes a computer failure to block the swap and challenges Finn to a sing-off, with the losing camp to close for good and surrender its land to the winner.

While the two girls learn to fit into unfamiliar worlds and make unexpected friends, Erika overhears Lady Anne's assistant, Clive, revealing the stakes and admitting he has bribed one of the judges, Svetlana Petranova of Camp Arabesque. The other judges are rock legend Allegra James and Prince Reginald of Thistlebrook. Learning that one camp will be lost, the campers of both sides decide to perform together rather than compete. Allegra and the prince abstain, and Svetlana names Camp Royalty the winner, but Finn and Lady Anne overrule the result, agreeing that rock and royalty can mix, and plan to merge the camps the next summer, while Courtney and Erika form a band with their friends called Rock 'N Royals.

Kelly Sheridan voices Courtney and Svetlana, with Bethany Brown, Alessandro Juliani and Kira Tozer among the cast. The songs include "What If I Shine" and the end-credits single "Raise Our Voices". The film's British launch was accompanied by a singing competition promoted with the girl group Little Mix and Nickelodeon.

Set in 2005, six years after the first adventure, the film finds Tai Kamiya restless and without direction: his friends have drifted apart, he cannot gather them for one of his soccer games, and he has no plans for the future. When a Kuwagamon tears through Odaiba, Tai races to the scene, and Agumon arrives to digivolve and fight back as the battle spreads to the airport. Watching the destruction and the injured bystanders, Tai is shaken by the realization that the DigiDestined's battles cause real harm. A new connection to the Digital World is letting through infected Digimon more powerful than before, and the children of the second series appear to have been overwhelmed. Supported by a government task force aided by Gennai, the group reunites, including Mimi, who returns from America, but Tai clashes with Matt, who insists that only they can protect people. When the Royal Knight Alphamon attacks, apparently hunting a mysterious new DigiDestined named Meiko Mochizuki and her partner Meicoomon, Matt pulls Tai out of his paralysis and their partners combine into Omnimon, yet Tai hesitates at the decisive moment and Alphamon escapes, while the enigmatic Hackmon watches from the shadows.

The film centres on Kion (Max Charles), the fun-loving younger son of King Simba (Rob Lowe) and Queen Nala (Gabrielle Union), who is happy that his sister Kiara (Eden Riegel) is the one destined to rule. While chasing a ball into the forbidden Outlands with his friend Bunga, a fearless honey badger (Joshua Rush), Kion lets loose a tremendous roar that drives off the hyenas of Janja's clan. Simba and Rafiki reveal that this is the Roar of the Elders, a power once held by Simba's uncle Scar, who lost it by using it for evil and destroying his Lion Guard. As the second-born, Kion must now lead a new Guard of the fiercest, bravest, fastest, strongest and keenest of sight.

Kion chooses his friends: Bunga as the bravest, the cheetah Fuli (Diamond White) as the fastest, the hippo Beshte (Dusan Brown) as the strongest and the egret Ono (Atticus Shaffer) as the keenest of sight. Simba is dismayed that his son has not picked lions, insisting the Guard is no game. Doubting himself and fearing he might turn out like Scar, Kion receives advice from the spirit of his grandfather Mufasa (James Earl Jones), who tells him to trust his instincts. Meanwhile, alerted by the vulture Mzingo, Janja plots to strike before the new Guard can form, and the hyenas start a stampede in a gazelle herd. Kion defies his father, bestows the Mark of the Guard on his friends, and leads them into battle; together they rout the hyenas, Bunga saves Kiara from a stampede, and Kion's roar drives Janja back to the Outlands, after which Simba accepts the new Lion Guard.

Ernie Sabella voices Pumbaa, alongside Kevin Schon as Timon, Jeff Bennett as Zazu and Khary Payton as Rafiki, while Sarah Hyland and Madison Pettis voice Kiara's friends Tiifu and Zuri. The film introduces the motto "Zuka Zama" as the Guard's counterpart to "Hakuna Matata".

Jack Stone is a good cop and family man whose wife was murdered on the orders of Balam, a cunning Russian crime lord who runs the city from behind bars and controls corrupt members of the police force. Balam lives in a lavish private cell deep inside a maximum-security prison, protected by loyal henchmen and guards, in a section of the facility that even the warden fears to enter. Determined to get close enough to take revenge, Jack deliberately gets himself convicted and sent to the same prison, through a staged bank robbery and the death of a fellow officer, one of the policemen on Balam's payroll. Once inside, he quickly runs afoul of guards who work for the kingpin, masked and armored, and of Balam's thugs, and beatings and backstabbing become a daily occurrence. His only ally is William, a seemingly slow, unassuming inmate who works as a janitor and keeps out of trouble, but who proves willing and able to watch his back. Meanwhile, in the women's wing, the tough inmate Alena keeps picking fights so that she will be sent to the infirmary, where she can slip loose to carry out a secret mission of her own, which turns out to be connected to William. The storylines converge in a violent prison riot during the final half hour, as Jack fights his way toward Balam.

Riot was released in 2015 and came out on Blu-ray and DVD by Universal in April 2016. Reviews from action-oriented outlets were moderately positive. Ian Jane of DVD Talk called it a predictable, generic but well-paced B-grade prison movie whose highlights are its plentiful, well-choreographed fights and the climactic riot, praising Reese as a credible action hero, Liddell's authentic moves despite an unconvincing Russian accent and Chuchran's physicality, while noting that Lundgren, though top billed, is underused. The Action Elite praised the physical performances of Reese and Chuchran and found Lundgren doing something different by moving into a nuanced character role.

Barbie (Kelly Sheridan) drives her younger sisters Skipper, Stacie and Chelsea in their pink camper to their childhood hometown of Willows for a two-week summer stay with Grandma Roberts. Her dog, Tiffany, has had four puppies who can talk among themselves, and each sister adopts one: Barbie takes Taffy, Skipper DJ, Stacie Rookie and Chelsea Honey. Rummaging in the attic, Skipper finds an old map, and Grandma explains that the town's founders buried a treasure to be found in a time of need so that Willows would always prosper. While Barbie plans to spend time with her childhood friend Christie at the Willowfest fair, the younger girls set off on the treasure hunt, unaware that two carnival workers, Joe and Marty, are following them in hopes of seizing the prize.

The trail of riddles leads the sisters and their puppies from the town hall to a founders' vase holding a willow-tree charm, to Lake Willows, a fountain and the musical town clock, whose chiming tune hides the next clue. Meanwhile Barbie notices that Willowfest has shrunk, shops have closed, the town is in disrepair, and Christie's family must move away because they can no longer afford to stay. After Joe and Marty steal Skipper's tablet with the girls' notes, Barbie joins the hunt. Following the map's song lyrics, the sisters find a hidden tunnel beneath the first willow tree, cross a cavern to an underground lake, and open a treasure vault with the charm. The crooks trap everyone inside with a rockslide, but Taffy frees them, and the puppies tie up the thieves before the police arrive.

The girls donate the treasure to the town, reviving Willows: shops reopen, repairs are made and Christie's family can stay. Before leaving with their puppies, the sisters hide part of their reward with a new map to give townspeople something to believe in. The voice cast includes Kazumi Evans as Skipper, Claire Maggie Corlett as Stacie, Alyssya Swales as Chelsea and Joanne Wilson as Grandma.

Katherine, the princess of the kingdom of Montsaurai, is in New York City during the holiday season on a grueling official tour managed by her strict aunt. All she wants is a single hour to visit an art museum, but her aunt will not hear of it, so when an opportunity arises, the princess slips away from her entourage and security detail to explore the city on her own. Early in her escapade, a thief steals her purse and her treasured camera, a gift from her late mother. The theft brings her into contact with Jack, a kind contractor who specializes in remodeling and restoration. Wary of involving the police and introducing herself under the alias "Katie", she tests her new independence but soon comes to rely on his help, while Jack, unaware of her true identity, shows the beautiful stranger his side of the city and his family, and his sister Emma lends her clothes. As they bond over a shared love of photography and the city, the royal household quietly hires a security specialist to find her, and Emma's ambitious boyfriend Ross, a television reporter, pursues the story of the missing princess as his ticket to the big leagues. Katie is eventually forced to reveal that she is royal, and the question becomes whether Jack will feel the same once he learns the truth. Before she returns home for her Christmas duties, he makes sure she finally gets her hour at the museum.

The film premiered on Hallmark Channel in late November 2015. Reviews were mixed. The blog Holiday Watch rated it 2.75 out of 5, finding that the elements never quite clicked, with obvious acting, little urgency, a predictable ending, an overbearing reporter character and limited chemistry between the leads. Viewer ratings described it as formulaic but warm and watchable, with Campbell's performance often singled out for praise.

At its core, All American Bikini Car Wash is a celebration of female camaraderie and the power of women supporting one another. The film showcases the strong bonds between the characters, particularly as they navigate the challenges of adulthood, love, and identity. Through their experiences, the movie highlights the importance of friendship and community in helping individuals find their place in the world.

The film also touches on themes of self-discovery and empowerment, as the characters learn to take control of their lives, pursue their passions, and assert themselves in a society that often seeks to hold them back. The movie's lighthearted tone and comedic moments belie its deeper exploration of these themes, making it a fun and engaging watch.

Overall, All American Bikini Car Wash is a heartwarming and entertaining film that celebrates the strength and resilience of women, while also offering a humorous and relatable take on the challenges of growing up.

After living for some years with her Aunt Dete, the orphaned Heidi is brought up into the Swiss Alps and left with her grandfather, a gruff recluse feared by the villagers below, who is far from pleased to have his solitude disturbed. The curious, cheerful girl soon wins him over, and she befriends Peter, a slightly older boy who herds goats, growing up happily in the mountains while longing to attend the village school.

Dete unexpectedly returns and tricks Heidi into leaving with her for Frankfurt, where she is to be a companion to Klara, the daughter of a wealthy family, who cannot walk and uses a wheelchair. With Klara's loving father often away on business, the household is run by the strict Fräulein Rottenmeier. Heidi struggles with reading and polite manners, but the two girls become close friends, and Klara's kindly grandmother encourages Heidi to learn to read. Heidi's homesickness grows until she begins sleepwalking at night, and the servants take her for a ghost. On the doctor's advice, she is sent home, leaving Klara hurt. Back in the Alps, her grandfather lets her go to school and takes a winter home in the village. When Klara later visits, a jealous Peter pushes her wheelchair off a cliff, but in the mountain air she gradually regains the use of her legs and surprises her father by walking, and Klara's grandmother gives Heidi a notebook to encourage her dream of becoming a writer.

Lilley plays Kate Jordan, a dedicated Boston lawyer whose devotion to work has left her with no lasting relationships and who has not really celebrated Christmas since her mother's death. Her boss gives her twelve days to close a deal: she is sent to Vermont to appraise the Hollygrove Inn so that it can be sold, a job she hopes will win her a promotion. On arrival she finds the caretaker, Walter Rafferty (Robert Walsh), uncooperative; he explains that the prospective buyer fled because a spirit lives in the house and disapproves of its sale, and that the inn cannot take guests because of the ghost. Kate soon meets the handsome Daniel Forsythe (Beaudoin), the owner of the mansion, who has been scaring off buyers. Murdered ninety-five years earlier, Daniel returns to the inn in bodily form for twelve days every Christmas, but he remembers neither who killed him nor why.

Kate puts the sale aside to help him. The two get off to a rocky start, with Daniel locking her out of the house and tossing blankets out after her, but they gradually warm to each other, and he even finds himself pressed into tending bar at a holiday party. As the days pass, they uncover the reason for his murder and the identity of the killer, and they fall in love, forcing Daniel to make a choice about his feelings before his time runs out. The supporting cast includes Bates Wilder as Sheriff Noah Bell, Kati Salowsky and Joanna Herrington.

Though it attracted less attention than many holiday television films on its release, the film has drawn admirers since. Writing for MovieWeb in 2022, Gissane Sophia called it a top-tier holiday film that had slipped under too many radars, praising the slow-burn romance between two jaded, heartbroken people, the leads' chemistry, Beaudoin's sardonic, brooding Daniel and the way the romance develops through solving the mystery, and arguing that it deserved cult status.
